Introduction: With the increasing availability of RNA-sequencing data, we can now not only study genome-scale transcriptomic changes but also single-cell distribution and location. One way to do this is by integrating massively parallel sequencing with spatial biology to compile spatial transcriptomic snapshots for each individual (e.g., Automated RNA Identifiers-RNAiMapper) to study transcriptional changes in localized cells.

Methods: We developed a dynamic volume reconstruction method that takes advantage of analytical performance of genome-scale gene expression data (GSNED), spatial clustering techniques (t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding; tSNE), and spatial volume and noise estimates to reconstruct cell-specific spatial volumes.

Results: We demonstrated that our method outperforms the 4-fold increase in memory for common cellular modules and has a 1.8-fold increase in training accuracy when compared to an estimation that relies on location from the genome-scale gene expression dataset. When analyzing cell type level data, we were able to demonstrate cell-specific transformations and also identify and manually identify the individual that expressed a given mRNA. Furthermore, we created a simple cell-specific pipeline to reconstruct spatial cell volume as a function of probe occupancy. Our model is agnostic to whether cells are located on a microfluidic chip or in vivo.

Conclusion: Our model of the organismal subcellular space is generalizable across a broad range of cellular organisms and cellular structures. The methodology developed here will allow researchers to look more deeply into the spatial organization of subcellular molecules to address current research questions in spatial transcriptomics, spatial genomics, and spatial modeling.

High-throughput single-cell microscopy offers the unprecedented opportunity to track changes in gene expression through changes in protein and RNA levels. However, the collective characterization of these changes demands the simultaneous localization of thousands of simultaneous biological processes. To address this challenge, we trained GRASP, a single-cell custom-built machine learning model for on-cell localization, on experimental data gathered in heterogenous conditions and spatial contexts. GRASP can be trained to locally localize individual single-cell data to gene expression or gene function time points. It can subsequently track gene expression across cells, from which it estimates which genes are turned on when neighbors change. Based on this approach, we identified many additional cell-types, cellular function, and transcriptomic hubs across a wide diversity of experimental conditions. We also developed a machine learning platform and prototype application to map cellular components in high-throughput single cell proteomics screens.

Single-cell analyses have sparked interest in understanding complex phenomena by identifying cell types, cell states, spatial locations, spatial interactions, etc., in single cells. However, achieving precision in such analyses, especially at a single-cell level, is challenging. While vast quantities of biological information can be systematically collected using an appropriate experimental design, single-cell analyses often force biological and statistical complexity into a fixed pipeline of basic workflows. It is a challenge to analyze single-cell data with a more comprehensive framework for relevant data analysis. In this study, we proposed to co-develop "Preprocessing - Integration - Accuracy - Deconvolution" as an integrated pipeline to facilitate the analysis of single-cell data and improve the reliability of single-cell analyses with a common tool. We used a single-cell RNA-seq pipeline to compare and illustrate the power of the proposed pipelines through comparisons with Fano and Time-Based Pipelines. We applied the proposed pipelines to 6 cell types and identified some limitations associated with traditional statistical approaches. This provides one of the first approaches to leverage single-cell data in enhancing the power of single-cell analyses.

In this work, a novel tool, Cell-SeqVis, has been created to visualize cell lineage information across cellular contexts and time. Cell-SeqVis enables the generation of comprehensive genome-scale visualisations of cell orderings with over 4 billion 4bp per cell partitions, representing 99% of all the human sequencing data from the UCSC Genome Browser. Cell-SeqVis leverages the powerful python-generated Genomics Packages Toolkit (GenPaT) workflow to provide long-read genome-scale cytogenetics. Cell-SeqVis presents spatial and temporal cell trajectories and hierarchy over complex cellular organisation in a single-image representation using a coherent combination of background scatter and voxcel background jets, allowing real-time visualisation of genomes with high dimensional correlation (e.g. ND array and single-cell RNA sequencing). The tool aims to serve as a tool for future studies to explore or manipulate cell information. Its visualisation architecture, the user-friendly pipeline and the powerful genomics toolkit are freely available online.

Single-cell genomics is revolutionising the field of Cancer Research. From understanding tumor heterogeneity to exploring the diversity of tumor microenvironments and driving diagnostics and immunotherapies. However, the accessibility of single-cell data poses significant challenges, notably hindering the development of biomarker-based models. Therefore, automated single-cell analysis technologies serve as pivotal solutions for this challenge. We developed a novel cell state-detection pipeline, Cellxpress, that automates and correlates single-cell high-dimensional images with cancer patient-derived cell properties, e.g., immunophenotypes and gene expression. Cellxpress combines single-cell image analysis with automated step-wise selection to identify candidate biomarkers for several breast and bowel cancer subtypes. Each cellstate is associated with an enzyme-based parameter, reflecting immune activation, inflammation, or epithelial state. Based on these parameters, an expert can interpret the final analysis in a fraction of the time needed for manual processing. Our pipeline ensures high inter- and intra-subject reproducibility, and its scalability to single-cell data sets allowing to enroll hundreds of samples. Cellxpress is currently implemented in several publicly available databases for immuno-oncology, e.g. ProteoBank, the Immune Earth, and UniProtID. In an in silico validation, Cellxpress was employed to predict further biomarkers like bisphosphonate and histone modification. Cellxpress was also validated in interdisciplinary clinical trials. Using single-cell data as an input is crucial for ensuring the viability of a diagnostic algorithm. We demonstrated that Cellxpress can also be used as a flow cytometer-independent automated assay to detect relapsed/refractory breast cancer patients, a disease with high relative survival rates but no unique biomarkers. We anticipate that Cellxpress has a promising future in personalized cancer medicine, with the ability to segment cancer patients based on disease-specific properties such as tumor immune response status or location within the disease. The integration of Cellxpress in clinical applications promises to provide comprehensive and precise analyses of breast and bowel cancer patient responses. Moreover, Cellxpress enables personalized approaches to immunotherapy testing, especially in immuno-oncology. All the main principles used in Cellxpress were published in detail in 2016.

Background Deep phenotyping enables the development of tailored cell models for drug screening, enabling a range of disease modeling, regenerative medicine, and translational research. Single-cell sequencing in many cell types provides an ideal platform to generate highly-resolved multi-dimensional phenotypes. Studies of single-cell suspensions will in turn facilitate highly-parallel cell line expansion, thus permitting a myriad of applications including the production of highly-pure phenotypes and cell lines, including highly efficient cell sorting methods. However, generating and cultivating single cells is currently an onerous and expensive process, especially for large consortia looking to examine hundreds or thousands of cells simultaneously.

Methods We leveraged a recently developed, validated single-cell image analysis software (Cellan/) to perform cost-efficient analysis of eight human cell lines across seven research institutions.

Results For this work, we developed and validated a low-cost method to perform a single-cell imaging data analysis, enabling high-throughput identification of high-quality data from >200K cells. We identified ∼4,000 gene co-expression signature modules and were able to quickly screen for gene expression clusters with cell-interchange. Remarkably, we are able to successfully re-analyze all of the analyses of our user-submitted, private sample (TET and TREG-78 cells), yielding a predicted transcriptional fingerprint of phenotypic identities and a cell line purity of 1.0% only three months after analysis.

Conclusion Our developed image analysis pipeline will enable single-cell phenotyping studies of new models and will allow for the automated and scalable evaluation of hundreds or thousands of cells. This approach will ultimately lower costs, expedite the growth of consented collections, and increase the accessibility of emerging single-cell, single-cell sequencing-based models to all researchers.

Key messages
1.Cellan/ is a low-cost analysis platform that provides a set of tools for automated multi-dimensional analysis of single-cell microscopy images.
2.Cellan/ has been utilized to analyze results from three projects aimed to generate a non-blank slate sample for downstream analysis, including: retargeting samples from a custom anti-β-GalNAc panel to identify common cell lines, screening for cell line purity using a pooled sample set, and a study analyzing the difference in cell line purity by identifying high-quality data from multiple sequencing methods.
3.Cellan/ enables analysis of non-blank slate samples and can be used to study thousands of cells simultaneously.

Congratulates author(s) Zhou, Hui

Large-scale, whole-genome or whole-transcriptome sequencing has revolutionized genome analysis across disciplines by enabling the search for new genes, complex genomic rearrangements, and regions of interest. However, the throughput of long sequencing projects (e.g., >20 Gb of data) is too slow for continuous data processing, making it expensive to scale to larger regions of the genome. To address this, we develop spatiotemporal sequencing (STS) by considering the sequencing of single cells as a single-cell sequencing panel. Like current single-cell sequencing panels, STS records the mRNA expression and transcription level of cells to obtain information about their identities and function. However, STS leverages time-series data of cells across a physical space of millions of cells as compared to the single cells in single-cell sequencing panels. Thus, STS exploits the performance of current sequencing technologies while using their space-limited expense. STS amplifies existing technological capabilities through our demonstrated capacity to assemble spatial datasets of cell transcriptomes using ESPPs, which we developed to generate spatiotemporal cellular profiles of multiplexed gene expression data, and the availability of parallel computing power to accelerate temporal processing of high-throughput gene expression data. Together, STS's integration of technology and informatics enables massive parallel and parallel-in-parallel sequencing to generate complete global transcriptomic profiles from cells across space in minutes.

Spatial resolutions are key to current sequencing technologies, shaping how research data is used. Traditional protocols, like nested PCR and gel electrophoresis, manually align reads across tissue sections, but these are computationally expensive. In this work we investigate alternatives, such as state-of-the-art point-of-care techniques with digital imaging systems, and a fully automated workflow through online datasets. In parallel, we curate microfluidic results into a curated pipeline with downstream adaptations and workflows, to facilitate meta-analysis and study interpretation. We apply point-of-care tools to single-cell RNAseq data from human lymphocytes, showing they can replace existing PCR methods for quantifying gene expression kinetics. We curate this data with a MATLAB based loss-based hyperparameter optimization framework, identifying inefficiencies with the gene correlation method. We have also implemented a novel immune cell gating method that efficiently identifies immune cell types in single cell datasets. Our pipeline, and hyperparameter optimization, enables unbiased comparisons and understanding of gene activity across tissue types. Our contributions could assist in a future AI model for gene quantification, combining automated optimization and artificial intelligence in a single workflow.

Serial cultivation of living cells is a key component of modern biotechnology, enabling continuous manufacturing of cellular products. Single-cell imaging captures the activity of tens to hundreds of thousands of cells within a well-defined spatial context. By using flow cytometry to identify and purify donors, we have leveraged the accuracy of the spatial resolution of serial cultivation on single cell identification. However, current protocols for flow cytometry require individual donor cells to be deposited in a mini-pillar flow chamber. In this study, we develop a new protocol to image and acquire flow cytometry data for single-cell cultivation, allowing more full-length approaches to be applied to live single-cell cultivation. Using the protocol, we generated gene expression data of all 319 donors and 296 single-cells prior to wild-type plate assay to quantify the spatial resolution of such data. Our protocol, coupled with MS spectrums, revealed a highly dynamic transcriptome at the single cell level.

Spatial transcriptomics (STXM) is an emerging tool that has been used to elucidate cell fate and cell behavior in cancer cells and tumors. However, the reasons for intratumoral variability and heterogeneity remain unclear, and it is likely that different cell types within tumors or different stages of cancer development express similar but distinct sub-populations of STMs. While recognizing this, many recent studies have attempted to discover sub-populations of STMs that can be used to monitor the temporal/spatial expression profile of STMs and determine those sub-populations that show dynamic changes in expression over time. However, the effectiveness of marker-based approaches to identify sub-populations of STMs is unclear. In this manuscript, we show that an all-silica NMR based process able to identify sub-populations of STMs is biologically plausible and can be readily applied on the Illumina RNAseq data. Accordingly, we demonstrate that our method yields multiple sub-populations of STMs that correspond to distinct transcriptomics patterns on Illumina short-read RNAseq data, and each sub-population presents different time-dependant alterations in STMs expression profile. We also apply our "STMseq" pipeline to investigate and identify Dicer in lung cancer, and show that Dicer proteins are expressed in sub-populations of basal, early and late stages of lung cancer and lung adenocarcinoma. Together, our findings provide a practical approach to identify sub-populations of STMs in DNA-based and RNA-based tumor profiling studies.
sample_p_texts: High-content cytometry is an important technique in clinical research, producing data that is rich and complex to analyze. The resulting clusters of cells must be profiled to determine their role and function, and analyzed to identify changes in cell frequency or marker intensity. The heat map is the most suitable tool for presenting this information in a synthetic way. However, its construction must be adapted to the information and the objective. Here we describe the step-by-step construction of heat maps of marker intensity and cell frequency using Excel, Phantasus or R, including the conversion of numbers to colors and the organization of rows and columns. Researchers who master these steps will be able to correctly interpret heat maps and derive the most benefit from high-content cytometry.

The diversity of cellular and tissue structures can arise from a few basic cell shapes, which undergo various transformations based on biophysical constraints on cytoskeletal organization. While cellular geometry has been linked with selected biological processes such as polarity, signaling or morphogenesis, the orchestration of the whole proteome in association to cell shape is still poorly understood. In this study, using more than 1 million images of single cells stained for 11,998 proteins across 10 cell lines in the Human Protein Atlas database, we performed an integrated analysis of organelle, pathway and single protein levels in association to a 2D cellular shapespace. We found that cell and nuclear shapes across cell lines exist in a shared continuum. We also found that the subcellular organelle topology varies across cell lines, but remains robust within each cell lines shapespace. At the single protein level, we found that cells of different shapes in the same cell cycle phase might be preparing for different fates, and that many non-cell cycle proteins expressed shape-based abundance variation. Using the same coordinate framework defined by shape, we could analyze the distribution shift of protein spatial localization under drug perturbation.

We report a cellular barcoding strategy, SpaceBar, that enables simultaneous clone tracing and spatial transcriptomics profiling. Our approach uses a library of 96 synthetic barcode sequences that can be robustly detected by imaging based spatial transcriptomics (seqFISH), delivered such that each cell is labeled with a combination of barcodes. We used these barcodes to label melanoma cells in a tumor xenograft model and profiled both clone identity and spatial gene expression in situ. We developed a gene scoring metric that quantifies how strongly gene expression is driven by intrinsic cellular cues or extrinsic environmental signals. Our framework distinguishes between clonal dynamics and environmentally-driven transcriptional regulation in complex tissue contexts.

Single-cell omics approaches profile molecular constituents of individual cells. Replicated multi-condition experiments in particular aim at studying how the molecular makeup and composition of cell subpopulations changes at the sample-level. Two main approaches have been proposed for these tasks: firstly, cluster-based methods that group cells into (non-overlapping) subpopulations based on their molecular profiles and, secondly, cluster-free but neighborhood-based methods that identify (overlapping) groups of cells in consideration of cross-condition changes. In either approach, discrete cell groups are subjected to differential testing across conditions; and, a low-dimensional cell embedding, which is in turn derived from a subset of selected features, is required to delineate subpopulations or neighborhoods.

We hypothesized that decoupling differences in cell type (i.e., between subpopulations) and cell state (i.e., between conditions) for feature selection would yield an embedding space that captures different aspects of cellular heterogeneity. And, that type-not-state embeddings would arrive at differential testing results that are comparable between clusterand neighborhood-based differential testing approaches. Our study leverages a simulation framework with competing type and state effects, as well as an experimental dataset, to evaluate a set of feature scoring and selection strategies, and to compare results from downstream differential analyses.

In the expanding field of spatial genomics, numerous methods have emerged to decode biomolecules in intact tissue. Advanced techniques based on combinatorial decoding can resolve thousands of features in a reasonable time but are often constrained by either the prohibitive costs associated with commercial platforms or the complexity of developing custom instruments. Alternatively, sequential detection methods, like single-molecule FISH, are easier to implement but offer limited multiplexing capability or signal amplification. Here, we introduce Cassini, a new approach for straightforward, cost-effective multiplexed measurements of mRNA and protein features simultaneously. Cassini leverages rolling circle amplification (RCA), known for its robust amplification and remarkable stability even after intense stripping, to serially detect each feature in under 20 minutes of total experimental time. The method also enables simultaneous immunostaining with either fluorophore-conjugated or DNA-barcoded antibodies, through an optimized immunostaining buffer. In a single overnight run, we show that Cassini can quantify 32 features (comprising both RNA and proteins) with sensitivity similar to state-of-the-art FISH techniques. We provide a comprehensive protocol alongside an online probe-design platform (cassini.me), aiming to enhance accessibility and user-friendliness. With our open-source solution, we aspire to empower researchers to uncover the nuances of spatial gene expression dynamics across diverse biological landscapes.

sample_q_texts: High temperatures accelerate mutation rates in plant cells in the response to disturbances of circadian rhythms, transcriptional programs, and environmental insults. Given their altered dormancy period in the heat, Arabidopsis thaliana inter-specific hybrids (ISI hybrids) yield lower heat-induced gene expression rates than antherbrood (BB) plants but they rapidly increase plant heat-responsive gene expression in the post-endothermic heat stress condition. Our long-term studies of the ISI hybrid revealed in-depth dynamic and integrative data about heat-induced gene expression, such as reduced expression of Arabidopsis heat-shock transcription factors during post-endothermic conditions. This natural state is genetically dissociated from the BB plant but not responsive to ABA signaling, and holds a collective memory of long-term light and temperature history. ISI hybrids respond to a high-temperature stress in a cell autonomous fashion with elevated gene expression. This cell autonomous plant response is stabilized by elevated transcriptional activity. The increased transcript levels are achieved by an extended promoter activity, reduced transcription-related gene activities, and shortened gene expression in response to heat. This data points out a novel and rapid plant adaptation mechanism to transient environmental perturbations, highlighting them as potential candidates for enhanced plant heat stress resistance.

Floral color divergence is widespread in angiosperms, and color formation is the first step in floral evolution and conversion from flowers to seeds. Floral color regulation could be affected by photoperiod or temperature but, in the wild, the response is multifactorial and complex. Here, we performed whole-genome sequencing from a mexican line of tomato flowers of four different geographic origins to gain insights on their gene expression landscape in flower color development during the lifecycle. We found many genes, such as LIRG1, g<sub>CS</sub>H<sup>+</sup>, and NSMCE, downregulated during flower color evolution, suggesting a loss of regulatory signals in flower color development. Using a combination of large phylogenomic, transcription factor (TF) and genotypic filtering strategies, we isolated candidate genes involved in this process. Finally, we used a genetic inverse-hybridization (GIGO) approach to ascertain which genes are differentially expressed in red-flowered plants compared to their correspondent red flowers (RdMs). Combining the two approaches revealed that some alleles of red-flowered tomatoes, which displayed a general interspecific similarity, were differentially expressed in all petals, without being truly red. The identified genes, including ND1, DAP1, and STRA1, which were expressed in both parents, we confirmed with bioinformatics tools. Altogether, our analyses revealed a regulatory landscape where pathway and network connections regulate color evolution through floral architecture.

The eukaryotic response to oxidative stress is characterized by a high degree of plasticity, with transcriptional programs that regulate the cellular response being well-conserved throughout the eukaryotic lineage. However, little is known about how regulation of the Cell Wall Genome-for example, transcriptional repression of cell wall genes is higher in plants than in animals has informed the design of regulatory elements that encode the cytoskeletal proteins connecting the cell wall's functional compartments (eg, the MW-like proteins.) In Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana), a phenomenon of limited significance in other organisms (e.g., grasses and algae) has been conserved for the MW-like proteins. The core subunit of a MW-like protein that makes a large, branched cytoskeleton in Arabidopsis and other angiosperms, the MW-like gene HpMpvT1, functions as a transcriptional repressor that directly binds and sequesters WT mRNA. The HpMpvT1-dependent pro-duction of the 5.8 kb-long HvW3A4 precursor protein, which is processed within the nuclear kernel of the plants that express HpMpvT1, is repressed by the HpMpvT1/WT complex, at least in quiescent stages of plant development. We have shown that the HpMpvT1-WT complex is required for vegetative wall growth, invagination, elongation, as well as for HSP70, an integral part of plant tolerance to oxidative stress. Because HpMpvT1-dependent transcriptional repression of AT2* genes in late stasis is strongly elevated in Arabidopsis, we have studied whether HpMpvT1-dependent suppression of gene expression by the HpMpvT1-WT complex can be transferred to transgenic Arabidopsis lines that lack the corresponding precursor protein, and whose genomes have lost this precursor. In mutants lacking 1-8 kb of the HpMpvT1-WT complex, an impairment of the actin cytoskeleton in plants that lack their MW-like proteins was found. This impairment caused a progressive appearance of focal W-shaped, rather than elongate, cell bodies in the absence of HpMpvT1, which we propose is a stress-induced phenotype triggered by the HpMpvT1-WT complex. This was particularly marked in the cases of knockout mutant, which were clearly accompanied by defects in the Quorum-sensing response in cells that lack the HpMpvT1-WT complex. These results reveal a new genetic mechanism mediating effective adaptation of actin cytoskeleton alterations caused by the HpMpvT1-WT complex to stress

Plant biology, particularly with respect to stress response, is limited by the complex genetic architecture of individual individuals. Yet, the elucidation of shared regulatory motifs within genetic families, leading to the unraveling of potential regulators, holds transformative potential in understanding key genes and mechanisms. Despite their significance, these motifs are the subject of several limitations, including a lack of genetic resources, limited structural information, and challenges in accessing and decoding data. This raises the critical question of whether the prevailing representation schemes are insufficient to bring useful information to bear. Here, we propose a model of intra-genomic regulation that provides a foundational framework within which to analyze plant genes related to potential stress responses. This framework, demonstrated for the key Arabidopsis stress gene, JAPP1, is more coherent, explanatory and well integrated with the Gene Ontology (GO) terms and functional and genomic data, compared to other, more limited models. Specifically, we observed that the model can better capture cellular processes such as photosynthesis, stress-signaling, and a reduced reliance on hormone-like signals. Our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art representations, showing meaningful improvement in gene set quality and specificity, whereas the primary inhibitory motif extends beyond only physiological signal transduction for JAPP1 and the entire plant genome. Importantly, our results indicate that the more limited regulatory signatures of other classic Arabidopsis stress genes, which are highly non-physiological and not well represented in the existing sparse repertoire, do not appear to influence genes acting through the JAPP1 promoter motif, rather resulting from its domain-specific effect. This paves the way for a more holistic genomic analysis of genetic aspects of plant biology.

Effects of early-life flowering in Arabidopsis thaliana have profound implications for the evolution of plant reproductive systems. At later stages of plant development, flowering is regulated by negative feedbacks arising from the circadian clock and repression of putative expression by the ethylene response factor. Previous research has illuminated the cellular basis for floral repression. Here, we analyzed phenology-related gene expression of floral pressure-sensitive traits in transgenic plants expressing Arabidopsis R-ARE1, which is involved in early-life flowering. We show that the timing of flower development is driven by promoter RNA activity. In the absence of floral pressure, Arabidopsis R-ARE1 and AtREA3 increase gene expression in its promoter regions and are triggered by the circadian clock to counteract the circadian clock-mediated suppression of plant growth. We find evidence of differential expression of gene products involved in linking circadian clock to flower development and demonstrate that BR 3 can significantly disrupt hypocotyl cotyledon development and flowering in R-ARE1-expressing plants. These findings demonstrate that the circadian clock acts upstream of phase expression during developmental events that take place before the end of each day.

Significance StatementThe circadian clock drives plant responses throughout its life, and a conserved molecular architecture underpins molecular interactions between the clock and genes coding for signals during the day and nighttime. Arabidopsis R-ARE1, one of many circadian clock component proteins, controls flower development in ways that overlap with those of the circadian clock. To shed light on the relationship between the circadian clock and early developmental events, we examined expression patterns in a R-ARE1-derived mutant, a large Arabidopsis gene for which mRNA is degraded early in development. In control plants, R-ARE1 is principally regulated in its promoter regions by nuclear clock oscillations, but R-ARE1 expression in night-active plants is suppressed by the circadian clock. Still, in the presence of a light period just before flowering, the clock shifts to drive up expression of R-ARE1 and the promoter regions of other clock-coding genes in a night-active mutant. These results implicate another mechanism, the circadian clock, for driving expression of R-ARE1 and the transcription of clock genes during plant development.

The fitness of plants, from small, quickly grown vegetables like lettuce and spinach, to large, relatively unchanged crops like soybean, greatly depends on the timing and frequency of plant flowering. A complex of hundreds of flowering genes is regulated by the light-dark clock, which detects changes in the amount of light available and the length of the photoperiod. Many over 50,000 genes are expressed in a flowering plant and the dynamic regulatory interactions between these genes lead to variable rates of flowering. To date, the widely accepted view of the flowering path is that either (i) a key gene is turned off one day and turned back on the following day, or (ii) a cascade of gene expression is activated, leading to in- and expression of hundreds of flowering genes. Here, we use recent technical developments to examine the gene expression of different species of Arabidopsis thaliana at different growth stages in a graphical, automated manner, using the genome-wide Light-Dark Association (LDA) for Arabidopsis. We show that flowering patterns in an Arabidopsis day-length-shifted (DL-treated) background depend on leaf age (AL) and are typically 10 times greater in DL-treated plants than in control plants. We estimate that the AL-dependent promoter clock used to initiate flowering is ∼85% universal, indicating that developmental timing occurs on a different scale than events of multiple branching of expression patterns (MBPs). Arabidopsis has 216 DoMA sections, of which 75 doMA isoforms are expressed in mature leaves. The expression of two additional, unidentified, early flowering-related DoMA isoforms is dramatically reduced during leaf senescence in the DL-treated background, suggesting a link between senescence and plant flowering. Our analyses demonstrate the need for more complex models to link the time and frequency of flowering with the characteristics of a specific development time.

Covalent modifications of chromatin regulate important biological processes and are essential for plant cell function. But few studies have comprehensively applied multi-omics data to guide detection of changes in chromatin states during early developmental growth.

Here, we utilized integrative GWAS, transcriptome, and epigenome sequencing to comprehensively explore putative novel chromatin modifications (norm) in plants. We uncovered a "T-DNA promoter" (T-for-T) with high copy number in Arabidopsis that controls endogenous T-DNA promoter silencing in vivo. We showed that T-DNA promoter silencing in T-for-T plants disrupts the host chromatin remodeling by recruiting ARID1A during mitosis to induce degradation of constitutive Arid1, resulting in the progressive formation of depletion of epigenetic information leading to decline in crop yield, which is related to the development of crop plants. We demonstrate that phenotypic information can assist in rare detection of chromatin modification alterations based on in silico unbiased transcriptional read counts of non-templated target RNAs in vivo. We demonstrate a potential discrimination mechanism for chromatin modification control in crop plants based on an integrated analysis of two multi-omics data sets, which provides a new path to understand crop plants' genome architecture by integrating high-throughput transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial information into single cell multi-omics.

Highlights

•Functionalized-TLD-regulated Arabidopsis T-DNA promoter silencing is crucial for plant growth.

•Out of 45 proposed loci, two genes were identified by multiomics correlation analysis.

•Low-level T-DNA silencing alters plant developmental stage, which is related to agricultural development.

•Multimode RNAseq/epigenomics/spatial data analysis significantly increases the discovery rate of chromatin modification.

•In light of plant functional genomics and operon sequencing data, refined chromatin modification enrichment and functional annotation of putative target RNAs is critical for the detection of chromatin modification alterations.

BackgroundMicroRNAs (miRNAs) play critical roles in plant development and serve as biomarkers of disease, pest, and fungal attack. CRISPR-Cas9-enabled clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR-Cas) offers a powerful tool for large-scale gene knockdown in both molecular and genomic contexts. This study quantitatively investigated the efficacy of CG-CPA-Cas as a novel plant CRIPSR-Cas9 system, compared to its native background. This platform allowed for the interrogation of host plant relationships and genetic architectures, yielding insights into the temporal dynamics of microRNA-mediated transcriptional regulation.

ResultsWe identified conserved gene pairs (n=1,388) in the nutrient deprivation- and pathogen-induced Arabidopsis thaliana repressome. Genome-wide analysis identified co-transcribed genomic regions corresponding to each putative repressome gene pair, thereby confirming predicted genetic connections. We verified the genetic stability of 16 candidate orthologous genes in the Arabidopsis thaliana nutrient- and pathogen-induced repressome by genotyping using the T-DNA insertion/deletion screening (TI-DS). The R-UHRACH and R-CNA2 genes both showed high fitness levels in nutrient-and pathogen-inducible repressomes, while the R-HLP2G gene showed intermediate fitness levels. These data suggest that Cas9 activity is sufficient to silence gene transcription and suggest that individual genetic strains of Arabidopsis may have partially overlapping functions in the nutrient- and pathogen-induced repressome.

ConclusionCG-CPA-Cas, both as a monomeric and in its inverse repeats with the AtCGNAPY1R CRISPR effector, allows for the generation of inducible CRISPR-Cas9 systems with high target specificity and broad tissue specificity compared to the native, highly redundancy-prone Cas9 disruption system.

NoteThis manuscript will appear in Plos Computational Biology Vol. 23 No. 8.

Grape vines with significantly higher levels of abscisic acid (ABA) accumulate during winter and early spring. To assess the role of abscisic acid-related signaling pathways in the control of dormancy, we observed the response of control and ABA-treated spring-budded grapevine seedlings in summer (mean seed number 2,678, SD 96) and the influence of long-term ABA applications on bud set during a cold winter (mean 60 days). In the laboratory, spring-budded vines were subjected to long-term ABA application (19.1 years), which inhibited germination. Seedling development and bud emergence were observed for a year-round. Results showed that, when L-ABA is present in the rootstock rootstock, the number of offspring and seed weight increase significantly, but it is more dependent on increasing temperature. In L-ABA-treated summer-budded grapevines, low-temperature treatments of 0 °C (day/night) resulted in 100% and 29.9% of the mean seed number and birth rate, respectively. In winter, winter-budded plants exhibited a 12.9% and 33.7% mean seed number and birth rate. However, the biddled plant in the L-ABA-treated spring-budded grapevine did not produce any viable seeds during L-ABA. The ABA expression was analyzed by polymerase chain reaction and the results revealed that 55% of the ABA expression gene was expressed in leaf, while it was lower in buds. Expression of about 800 genes of the ABA pathway was upregulated in 8-week-old plants after L-ABA application. The present study showed that L-ABA-induced genes that responded to signal imbalances in early spring to late winter were also produced in winter-budded plants by long-term L-ABA application, which may lead to the loss of buds during cold winter.

Cell death in plants represents a developmental and physiological critical event. In particular, programmed cell death is observed during rapid development, plant growth and flowering in conditions of fluctuating nutrient availability. At maturity, plant survival may also require a cell death program. However, how cell death programs in plant responses to fluctuating energy supplies are connected to the developmental programme of leaves and their functions in the same plant remains uncertain. Understanding the role of cell death in modulating the vital character of leaf growth is critical to support targeted metabolic regulation during plant growth and development. Previously, we have identified two Arabidopsis alleles differing in caspases 12 and 8 by a recently characterized transcriptomic tool, targeting a set of 400 transcriptional start sites. To investigate how two alleles of caspases 12 and 8 influence leaf growth we profiled transcriptomes at four developmental stages using PCR array technique and found that the alleles are expressed differently in leaves of crucifer species. We found marked over expression of inhibitor and activators of caspases 12 and 8 in leaves, compared to wild type leaves. In particular, we found that while Actin is heavily expressed, CSP7, ATF20, and ELR1 are only weakly expressed in the leaves of caseinate resistant violaceolaceous plant (ViCV<sub>BP1</sub>) compare to the wild type. A semi-quantitative study using an independent mutant, CV<sub>BP</sub> observed that wild-type leaves exhibited overexpression of CSP7, while the RNAi-overexpressing plants showed over expression of inhibitor and activator caspases 12 and 8 enzymes. We also observed a differential expression pattern in other plant genes. Taken together these results provide evidence that two caspases 12 and 8, both involved in programmed cell death pathways, is involved in regulating leaf growth in planta. This suggests that the ability to express these enzymes in vivo may be relevant to plant responses to fluctuating energy supplies. Further, a comparison of maize's caspases with ViCV<sub>BP</sub> indicated significant variations in their expression levels, highlighting the importance of physiological and genetic diversity within plant species for improving potential for agricultural applications.
sample_p_texts: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone that controls a wide array of physiologically relevant processes, including plant responses to biotic and abiotic stress, and induces ripening in climacteric fruits. To monitor ethylene in plants, analytical methods, phenotypic assays, gene expression analysis, and transcriptional or translational reporters are typically employed. In the model plant Arabidopsis, two ethylene-sensitive synthetic transcriptional reporters have been described, 5xEBS:GUS and 10x2EBS-S10:GUS. These reporters harbor a different type, arrangement, and number of homotypic cis-elements in their promoters and thus may recruit the ethylene master regulator EIN3 in the context of alternative transcriptional complexes. Accordingly, the patterns of GUS activity in these transgenic lines differ and neither of them encompasses all plant tissues even in the presence of saturating levels of exogenous ethylene. Herein, we set out to develop and test a more sensitive version of the ethylene-inducible promoter that we refer to as EBSnew (abbreviated as EBSn). EBSn leverages a tandem of ten non-identical, natural copies of a novel, dual, everted, 11bp-long EIN3-binding site, 2EBS(-1). We show that in Arabidopsis, EBSn outperforms its predecessors in terms of its ethylene sensitivity, having the capacity to monitor endogenous levels of ethylene and displaying more ubiquitous expression in response to the exogenous hormone. We demonstrate that the EBSn promoter is also functional in tomato, opening new avenues to manipulating ethylene-regulated processes, such as ripening and senescence, in crops.

C4 photosynthesis has evolved in over sixty plant lineages and improves photosynthetic efficiency by [~]50%. One unifying character of C4 plants is photosynthetic activation of a compartment such as the bundle sheath, but gene regulatory networks controlling this cell type are poorly understood. In Arabidopsis a bipartite MYC-MYB transcription factor module restricts gene expression to these cells but in grasses the regulatory logic allowing bundle sheath gene expression has not been defined. Using the global staple and C3 crop rice we identified the SULFITE REDUCTASE promoter as sufficient for strong bundle sheath expression. This promoter encodes an intricate cis-regulatory logic with multiple activators and repressors acting combinatorially. Within this landscape we identified a distal enhancer activated by a quintet of transcription factors from the WRKY, G2-like, MYB-related, IDD and bZIP families. This module is necessary and sufficient to pattern gene expression to the rice bundle sheath. Oligomerisation of the enhancer and fusion to core promoters containing Y-patches allowed activity to be increased 220-fold. This enhancer generates bundle sheath-specific expression in Arabidopsis indicating deep conservation in function between monocotyledons and dicotyledons. In summary, we identify an ancient, short, and tuneable enhancer patterning expression to the bundle sheath that we anticipate will be useful for engineering this cell type in various crop species.

The Arabidopsis splicing factors arginine/serine-rich zinc knuckle-containing proteins 32 and 33 (RS2Z32 and RS2Z33) are plant-specific members of the SR family whose molecular functions received little attention. Here, we characterized both RS2Z32 and RS2Z33 by examining their expression profile at different stages of development and their spatial cellular distribution, as well as the contribution of their domains in the establishment of protein-protein interactions and RNA binding specificity. We report that the RS2Z32 and RS2Z33 promoters are ubiquitously active during vegetative and reproductive growth, and that both RS2Z splicing factors localize in the nucleus (except the nucleolus). We show that the C-terminal arginine/serine-rich (RS) domain, but not the serine/proline-rich (SP) extension, is a determinant of nuclear localization, which likely requires phosphoresidues putatively phosphorylated by kinases of the SRPK family. We demonstrate that their RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain specifically binds pyrimidine-rich RNA motifs via three residues (Y14, Y46, F48), and is also involved in protein-protein interactions with at least three SR proteins, namely SR45, SCL30, and SR34. Finally, we show that mutations in RNA-binding domains (i.e. RRM and zinc knuckles, ZnKs) affect the nucleocytoplasmic dynamics of both RS2Z proteins. Our findings provide molecular evidence for the involvement of plant-specific SR splicing factors into the regulation of the splicing process.

HighlightSpecific domains of the Arabidopsis RS2Z splicing factors contribute to their nuclear localization, nucleocytoplasmic dynamics, and ability to contact protein partners and specific pyrimidine-rich RNA motifs.

Temperature plays a crucial role in plant growth and development, influencing numerous physiological processes throughout the plant life cycle. Ambient temperature fluctuations can significantly affect transcriptomic adjustments, which are essential for plants to adapt to ever-changing environmental conditions. Despite the known impacts of extreme temperatures on plant physiology, there remains a knowledge gap regarding the specific effects of moderate changes in ambient temperatures on transcriptomic responses. This study employs strand-specific mRNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to assess how different splicing-related mutants respond to varying ambient temperatures, providing a valuable resource to the research community. Analysis of our time-resolved temperature-regulated alternative RNA splicing data reveals that common and exclusive use of the splicing machinery plays pivotal roles in thermoresponsive growth. Furthermore, our analyses demonstrate that moderate temperature changes are translated into widespread transcriptomic responses, including adjustments of the circadian clock and significant splicing changes in light and temperature genes. These results highlight the importance of these particular signaling pathways in adapting to new temperature regimes and suggest future experiments to study the role of alternative RNA splicing in temperature adaptation. Taken together, our results provide insights regarding the role of RNA splicing in plant responses to ambient temperature changes, highlighting the biological relevance of transcriptomic adjustments in enhancing plant resilience and adaptation to climate variability.

SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT- This is the first comprehensive study on how mutants involved in multiple steps of the splicing process modulate splicing activity in response to low and high ambient temperature changes.
- We assessed early and acclimated transcriptomic responses and created a valuable resource to investigate the biological outputs.

In Arabidopsis, a family of five receptors mediates ethylene responses in roots, with Ethylene Response 1 (ETR1) controlling increases in root hair proliferation and decreases in lateral root formation. To define the ETR1-dependent gene regulatory network (GRN) controlling root development, we profiled the root transcriptome from Col-0 and the etr1-3 gain-of-function and etr1-7 loss-of-function mutants in the presence and absence of ethylene or the ethylene precursor aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid (ACC). We identified 4,522 differentially expressed (DE) transcripts in Col-0 roots with altered abundance in response to ethylene and/or ACC treatment, most with larger magnitude changes induced by ethylene. These included 553 DE transcripts that were ETR1-dependent, defined by a lack of response to treatment with ethylene and/or ACC in ethylene-insensitive etr1-3 and constitutively altered in etr1-7 in the presence and absence of treatment relative to untreated Col-0. Within these ETR1 dependent transcripts were ethylene biosynthesis genes and transcription factors. ACC OXIDASE 2 (ACO2) and ACO3 convert ACC to ethylene and were ETR1-dependent, and ACO promoter fusions were ACC regulated in root tissues in appropriate locations to control root development, with ACO5 localized to root hairs. Abundance of ETR1-dependent transcripts that were predicted to encode transcription factors and ACOs were examined in Col-0 and an ein3eil1 mutant with and without ACC treatment, revealing that the ETR1 and EIN3/EIL1 canonical ethylene signaling pathway regulated some, but not all, of these transcriptional responses. Together, these findings reveal features of an ETR1-dependent GRN that controls both ethylene synthesis and root growth and development.

Infilitration of Agrobacterium tumefaciens into Nicotiana benthamiana has become a foundational technique in plant biology, enabling efficient delivery of transgenes in planta with technical ease, robust signal, and relatively high throughput. Despite transient expressions prevalence in disciplines such as synthetic biology, little work has been done to describe and address the variability inherent in this system, a concern for experiments that rely on highly quantitative readouts. In a comprehensive analysis of N. benthamiana agroinfiltration experiments, we model sources of variability that affect transient expression. Our findings emphasize the need to validate normalization methods under the specific conditions of each study, as distinct normalization schemes do not always reduce variation either within or between experiments. Using a dataset of 1,813 plants collected over three years, we develop a comprehensive model of variation in N. benthamiana transient expression, using power analysis to determine the number of individual plants required for a given effect size. Drawing on our longitudinal data, these findings inform practical guidelines for minimizing variability through strategic experimental design and power analysis, providing a foundation for more robust and reproducible use of N. benthamiana in quantitative plant biology and synthetic biology applications.

Plants coordinate growth and development with environmental signals. Specifically, temperature and photoperiod are important regulators to time the transition from vegetative to floral growth. Through utilising these environmental signals potential reproductive success is optimised, which is critical for the production of high crop yields. For cereals, some require a winter before undergoing reproductive development. This extended period of cold exposure enables the process of vernalization and is also important for the synchronised timing of the floral transition. The cereal-specific floral repressor VERNALIZATION2 (VRN2) has an integral role in this pathway, yet this locus remains poorly characterised in hexaploid wheat. Our research in a facultative wheat suggests that the tandemly duplicated genes comprising the VRN2 locus, ZCCT1 and ZCCT2, respond to multiple environmental factors and have differences in gene expression patterns at a gene and sub-genome level. These genes also show co-regulation, forming a regulatory loop between ZCCT-D1 and ZCCT-D2. The function of these genes beyond the classic vernalization response is explored in a facultative wheat with VRN-D2 identified to regulate early tiller development, with an accelerated rate of secondary tiller emergence and presence of coleoptile tillers. This phenotype increases ground coverage more rapidly, which provides agronomic benefits including improved competition with biological stressors. The findings identify that the VRN2 loci in bread wheat is formed of multiple genes which have overlapping but also unique regulation and function. Selecting these genes individually may offer a route to alter wheat plant architecture without directly impacting vernalization requirement.

To identify novel genes engaged in plant epidermal development, we characterized the phenotypic variability of rosette leaf epidermis of 310 sequenced Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, focusing on trichome shape and distribution, compositional characteristics of the trichome cell wall, and histologically detectable metal ion distribution. Some of these traits correlated with climate parameters of ourq accessions locations of origin, suggesting environmental selection. A novel metal deposition pattern in stomatal guard cells was observed in some accessions. Subsequent GWAS analysis identified 1546 loci with protein sequence-altering SNPs associated with one or more traits, including 5 genes with previously reported relevant mutant phenotypes and 80 additional genes with known or predicted roles in relevant developmental and cellular processes. Some candidates, including GFS9/TT9, exhibited environmentally correlated allele distribution. Several large gene families, namely DUF674, DUF784, DUF1262, DUF1985, DUF3741, cytochrome P450, receptor-like kinases, Cys/His-rich C1 domain proteins and formins were overrepresented among the candidates for various traits, suggesting epidermal development-related functions. A possible participation of formins in guard cell metal deposition was supported by observations in available loss of function mutants. Screening of candidate gene lists against the STRING interactome database uncovered several predominantly nuclear protein interaction networks with possible novel roles in epidermal development.

In many species, FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT)-like genes promote the floral transition by integrating environmental signals, in particular photoperiod, and internal cues. Here we show that Brassica napus contains 6 FT-like genes and 2 pseudogenes belonging to 3 orthogroups. All B. napus FT-like genes induce early flowering when expressed at the shoot apical meristems of Arabidopsis thaliana ft mutants, but BnaFT.C6 and non-orthologous FT-like genes do not encode fully functional mobile florigens. In the case of BnFT.C6, the functional change is associated with a T to C amino acid change that is restricted to semi-winter accessions. Expression of orthologs of FT is photoperiod-dependent and two distal enhancers are conserved; however, the homeologs BnaFT.A7 and BnaFT.C6 show rearrangements of DNA motifs binding NF-Y/CO and NF-Y transcriptional activator complexes between the promoter and downstream enhancers. Motif rearrangements correlate with differences in tissue-specific expression. Furthermore, homeologs with rearranged motifs could not be trans-activated by B. napus CO in transient assays although they genes show LD photoperiod-dependent expression. We propose that differential diurnal expression of NF-Y genes contributes to the photoperiod-dependent regulation of B. napus FT genes.

Significance statementB. napus FT-like genes are a case study for gene retention and retraction after multiple rounds of polyploidisation. Retained B. napus FT-like genes show preferred expression in different developmental stages and amino-acid changes that affect florigen function.

PremiseAs the sister clade to angiosperms, gymnosperms are key to enabling the reconstruction of ancestral gene regulatory networks for seed plants. However, tools to rapidly and efficiently investigate gene function in gymnosperms remain limited due to the challenges of long life cycles and large genome sizes. Species within the xerophytic genus Ephedra (Gnetales) have comparatively smaller genomes and shrubby growth habits with shorter life spans, making them better suited for greenhouse cultivation and laboratory experiments.

Methods and ResultsHere, we implement Virus-Induced Gene Silencing (VIGS) to manipulate gene expression in Ephedra tweedieana. Agrobacterium-mediated vacuum infiltration of Tobacco Rattle Virus (TRV2 and TRV1) in seedlings resulted in highly efficient silencing of the E. tweedieana PHYTOENE DESATURASE ortholog EtwPDS. The expected photobleaching phenotype was observed as early as two weeks. It lasted at least three months, in stems, shoot tips, leaves, axillary meristems, and lateral branches of treated plants.

ConclusionsThis first report of transient transformation and targeted gene silencing in a gymnosperm will further enable functional studies of the genetic mechanisms underpinning adaptations in this important and underrepresented lineage of seed plants.

Comparing genomic data from two populations of species with different reproduction rates can be an efficient approach to detect adaptation to environmental heterogeneity. Here we demonstrate that in addition to the conventional approach of nucleotide-level substitution rates, genomic sequence data can also be directly analyzed in terms of substitution rates using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. In addition, when morphologically contrasting populations are common, the MCMC-based population baseline model can be applied to investigate how many alleles for any given locus vary as a population may experience rapid range shifts or selection pressures. We show that the population baseline function allows for the simultaneous analysis of orthologous, convergent, and divergent allele frequencies within populations and between populations, effectively quantifying the strength of candidate selection. We applied this framework to natural evolution of mating system evolution and adaptation. Our results showed that polymorphisms in morphology-based reproductive traits and variation in alleles supporting polymorphisms are both important for population baseline estimation. Both morphologically-defined lineages in these populations diverged as a result of selective constraints on gene flow, rather than through adaptive genetic changes. The latter can be explained by divergence in the mating systems that is specific to the home state. Our results can serve as a framework for analyzing macroevolutionary processes driven by an underlying genetic adaptation.

IMPORTANCEHuman adaptation is subject to environmental diversity of both genes and organisms. As an aid for studying the process of adaptation, accurate and quantified measure of genetic diversity and evolution is needed. Recently, target species pairs which are typically very different in morphology have been used to assess the evolutionary history of morphological traits and gene systems. This method has been shown to be effective. Here, we demonstrate that common practice of quantitative genotyping and estimation of genetic diversity can be a powerful method of extracting most of the information in the population dynamics data.

Vegetation serves many functions, providing resources and habitat, yet can fail to evolve as expected due to external selection pressures. Within gene flow, populations can be more closely or less closely related to each other. The apparent complexity and indeterminacy of biotic interactions is a driver of divergence and potentially increases potential conservation potential. We use genomic data from plants across the Mediterranean region to evaluate how the historical patterns of competitive interactions, habitat use, and population genetic differentiation have influenced population divergence. We test for three levels of association between gene flow and divergence (local equilibrium, maladaptation, and adaptation). Our quantitative analysis showed that adaptation explains a significant proportion of genetic divergence between populations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adaptive nucleotide changes explain the major phylogenetic relationships we found between populations, but that habitat and local environmental conditions strongly influence the variability of the inferred genotypes. Local and environmental conditions are likely to influence population divergence. Future work should consider how different phylogenetic and geographic distributions shape the shape of divergence in these species. Understanding the causes and consequences of habitat adaptations and selection will allow for more efficient conservation efforts and adaptive management of species under anthropogenic pressures.

The first identified genes were inherited in a specific way. Later they were estimated to have a frequency of 100%. Nevertheless, it is unclear whether shared inbreeding with related, unrelated, or maternal lineages provided this common ancestor. To address this question, we assessed the stability of and likelihood that shared ancestors were of different species, clonal or evolutionary lineages of the same species. We generated detailed data of extant coprored and morphologically related species for multiple lineages of insects, reptiles, birds and mammals. We found that high congruence of gene haplotypes was observed across 14 phylogenetic branches for the members of the Collembola. These observations suggest that shared ancestry due to past adaptive shifts had a similar impact on extant species and were therefore spatially and temporally most stable. Furthermore, we have compared the stability of shared ancestry via the modeling of theoretical and empirical evidence. We show that shared ancestry (i) suffices, but is insufficient to explain the stability of shared haplotypes in some animal lineages. We also show that shared ancestry was sufficient to model ancestral pairing in terms of chromosome copying and introgression. Finally, we extend our analytic approach of projecting inferred haplotypes onto a sequence for multi-taxon gene models using simulation-based, forward-modeling.

The adaptation of haplotypes from ancestral states to local environments can generate genomic variability under selective pressures in response to changing environments. Here, we investigate the role of heteroplasmy in the evolution of passerine bird genomes and identify the genomic underpinnings of hybrid speciation among three families of passerines. We report evidence for a strong dependence of recent genome diversification patterns across the passerine bird lineages on levels of recessive heteroplasmy in these regions of the genome. Data show that heterozygous substitutions usually occurred more rapidly than null substitutions. Evolutionarily significant neutral variants (NESVs) involved in the accumulation of repetitive domains occurred faster on reduced mutation rates than those involved in non-replicated introgressed haplotypes. We propose that heteroplasmy promotes the accumulation of NESVs that are not synonymous to make use of mobile parts of the genome and accelerates diversification in response to changing environments.

Using sequencing of multiple loci simultaneously, the current methods to estimate the evolutionary lineage relationships (i.e., parsimony) between lineages, or distinguish their evolutionary rate variations, is of great importance for biodiversity studies, e.g., tracing the global patterns in diversity and phylogenetics. Yet, the genetic variability/variation among lineages is often neglected in the branch length estimates, and therefore, is termed "population genetic variability" (PGA), which is responsible for the disproportionate impact on the phylogenetic tree stability. In this study, we derive the PGA directly from the molecular genetic data, and quantify the sampling uncertainty introduced by the imperfect selection across loci. It shows that PGA is considerably overestimated by the existing methods. We further derive the PGA scale with the lineage-scale real-life conservation. It helps elucidate the important role of genomic selection on the population diversity and in the stability of the phylogeny. We argue that PGA is not only crucial to answer the “how much” of biodiversity, but also the “how much” it is affected by genomic selection.

Graphical abstract

OpenData: Figures, time and all data files and codes for these research papers are available at the corresponding author's github page.

The key determinant of how individuals of the same species vary with each other biologically is influenced by their shared environmental experiences. Hence, to understand the impact of non-genetic differences among individuals on phenotypic variation and its evolutionary consequences, lineage-dependent processes must be taken into account. To address this gap in our understanding, we examined the evolution of complex body forms among the spider lizard family (Leiocephalidae). This adaptive diversification results in diverse body shapes and sizes across different species. In a natural experiment at the local level, the ecological and historical features of the site in western Europe shape the diversification and related phenotype. If such non-genetic differences were shaped by an intrinsic trait, subsequent evolutions would reflect population-specific genetic differences. Therefore, in this work we compiled whole genome data from 736 individuals from seven populations across the Western Mediterranean for the first time, to test whether allopatric lizard populations are mirror-matched phylogenetically. We discovered very large random changes in genome size, a signature of selection. These changes would be likely to follow rapidly-occurring environmental change in the form of climate change. Furthermore, we observed a local founder effect, whereby new populations established in local basins were copied in other basins. The whole genome data from the pre-outbred lizards reveal a supergene tree, suggesting recurrent and lateral gene flow, which does not fit with molecular phylogeny, but with two non-random populations established in separate geographical regions. Future work will examine how different patterns of evolution with regard to shared and non-shared factors shape and determine phenotypic variation along the evolutionarily distinct lineages.

Understanding individual life history traits of amphibians such as herpetofaunal species is critical for conservation. To understand the evolutionary trade-offs that shape these traits, population genetic variation over species are investigated. Understanding the biology underlying variation at these levels is also critical to informing modern conservation strategies for amphibians. Here, we used haplo-summing to compare molecular genetic variation across 1,258 individuals representing nine synapomorphic morphotypes of three distinct morphological types of desert salamanders collected in the southwestern United States. We first determined a small number of neutral alleles within each morphotype, which we selected as evolutionary candidates for conservation efforts due to the phylogenetic relatedness within evolutionary lineages. Second, we characterized genetic differentiation, diversity, and population structure at the morphotypes, maintaining a minimum of 30 samples per population to estimate genetic diversity. Our results show variation across morphological types but suggest that phenotypic variation is associated with allopatry between morphotypes, despite having no apparent geographical contiguity between morphotypes. Overall, our results show that allopatry is a strong evolutionary driver of morphotype evolution, which is likely used to facilitate rapid specialization in morphology.

HighlightsAllopatry models predict genetic differentiation similar to polygenic variance between allopatric morphotypes.

Our results show that the molecular genetic make-up of desert salamanders may be the key to better-informed conservation.

Diversity models are needed to inform conservation efforts.

Polyploidy implies the multiplication of nuclei due to a constitutive increase of chromosome number by mitotic replication. Allopolyploidy results from a fusion of two populations with diverse ploidy levels and a rapid amplification of a hybrid genome through genome doubling. The frequency of both allelic and genome doubling processes is mainly dictated by the parent populations, but also occurs in and is caused by the progenitor and founder lineages, which may evolve, along with the species. Here, we propose the use of artificial population histories for inferring the frequency of allelic and hybrid genome doubling events in samples of extant multicellular species, based on their genomic duplication rates. To this aim, we used six aligned, publicly available genome sequences from seven species representing key nodes in the evolution of modern organisms, which we refer to as the 'Metacommunity Data Set', and then classified the data accordingly to five pairwise merging rules (simpler rules with smaller added sets of overlaps). Using simulation simulations, we derived a broad range of null hypotheses to test whether the parent populations always (by far) or ever had a clear dominance and majority decision. For the five- and 5+1 rules, the adult tree collapsed, as expected. Analyses based on local set sizes (limits of the training data sets) or one size only (true parsimony) also highlighted the dominance of one parent over the other. However, this dominance is often limited, occurring mainly after a second founder-originating lineage emerged and experienced disproportionate genome expansion or diversification. For the largest sets, it was difficult to detect dominance or diversity. Consequently, it was unclear which population gave rise to the vast majority of the lineage. Indeed, we conclude that diversification of the ancestral lineages probably occurred in most instances.

The Evolution of Insect Mating Behavior fits a continuous branching tree; arboreally, cold weather imposes functional selection on larval physiology and morphological traits, whereas hot weather necessitates both altered activity and heightened responsiveness. An adaptive trade-off exists between a sexually mature insect's behavior when foraging to detect a female and that desired by a male while the latter ensures successful copulation. While small insects have several sexual or hybrid forms, larger insect species evolved specialized 'conventional' forms to enhance efficient mating behavior in hot and humid climates, which also maximize the number of females fertilizing the male. Thus, "mating adaptations" confer distinct reproductive benefits, demonstrating that not all changes in insect behavior are purely random or individually neutral. In the lacewing Chalcosoma poniatini we recently introduced a "convergent trait detection" protocol for phylogenetic inference, including detection of the criteria used in behavioral ancient DNA analyses. This method allows us to understand the fitness of lineages based on their ancient phylogenetic relationships while faithfully detecting biases in ancestral patterns. We applied this approach to ancient transcriptomes spanning two weeks, comparing genetic variation between moth-like lineages and their ancestral lineage. At the family level, we detect convergence in both active trap larvae (A: trails) and "vigorous" behavior (B: predator avoidance and stinging). Higher divergence between "vigorous" and "notasvigorous" pairs indicates that ancestral patterns better capture the fitness of this divergent lineage than "notasvigorous" pairs. However, this evidence for convergent behavioral plasticity cannot be extrapolated to the species level as ancestral patterns mainly predict better ancestral dispersal abilities. Although ancestral patterns were more phylogenetically coherent than based on "clade 4" and "clade 5" pairs, they were also less diverse. Our results suggest that ancestral patterns better capture the efficacy of ancestral adaptations than ancestral traits.

Highlights
For the past 20 years, we have used a combined pedigree approach, DNA hybridization, and ancient transcriptomics to reconstruct the evolutionary past and the phylogenetic relationships of taxonomically diverse lineages. The combined approaches permit the detection of our selective characterizations and associated evolutionary trades.
Modern insects, like modern man, have "cultural" traits, e.g. that the ability to find a mate in time is highly valued.

Bird taxonomy is inherently fragmented due to high rates of species range differentiation along altitudinal gradients. However, studies that have directly addressed the variation of avian species traits along altitudinal gradients have been limited by the lack of explicit knowledge of the genetic basis of taxonomic barriers. This study integrated phylogenetic and genomic resources to map the avian genetic background underlying such barriers. We leveraged itsorely dissimilarity based on eight bird species- including ten million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and complete genomes for only five additional species. For the analysis, we developed a novel algorithm capable of automatically generating reference structures based on Phylogenetic Tree Inference (PTI) pruned with coalescent trees as input. The genome-wide association study (GWAS) we performed revealed significant shifts in genetic architecture for two bird species across North and South America. In Coelosphaera macellaria, a narrowly flushed Eurasian species, the resulting gene trees divide into five local tree groups within Europe, and two separate global tree groups with different shapes. In Platycanthus maculatus, which also extends across Eurasia and largely south to Mexico, the phylogenetic analysis indicates a clade-wide shift to the endomycorrhizal endoparasitic species with a long, thin, rightward branch in Eurasia. Using the GIPS (Groupe d'Indagation au Parlamephale de Sibi Electroniques) index, we found several genes candidates for being strongly influenced by the two migration events. Finally, using a gene-based model we confirmed that expansion of the western branch across the Atlantic occurred primarily in Europe and then spread to northern Central and South America.
