AimGenetic diversity contains valuable information about ecological and evolutionary aspects of species, such as historical demography. Intraspecific genetic variation is shaped by species natural history traits and by characteristics of geography and climate within their ranges. Salamanders (Order Caudata) are amphibians of ecological and conservation interest because of their global distribution, trait diversity, and roles within ecological communities. Here, we studied genetic variation within salamanders to investigate predictors of nucleotide diversity and spatial patterns of genetic differentiation.

LocationGlobal.

Time PeriodPresent.

Major Taxa StudiedSalamanders.

MethodsWe repurposed mitochondrial DNA sequences, natural history traits, and geographic and environmental data from open-access databases for 214 salamander species. We calculated nucleotide diversity ({pi}) and tested for isolation by distance (IBD) and isolation by environment (IBE) within each species. We analyzed these three response variables with random forest analyses and phylogenetic comparative methods using 27 predictors expected to be associated with genetic variation (e.g., number of offspring, total range size).

ResultsWe recovered 8,175 Cytb sequences with their associated geographic coordinates, of which 7,007 sequences were manually curated by us. Species range size and sample size (the number of sequences) were important predictors of genetic variation. We found higher diversity in regions including the Neotropics and central-eastern Europe. The absence of strong phylogenetic signal in {pi}, IBD, and IBE suggests that genetic variation is shaped by local ecological and geographical factors rather than by shared ancestry.

Main ConclusionsOur finding that range size was an important predictor of genetic variation aligns with theoretical expectations that species with larger ranges tend to harbor more genetic diversity. Our results underscore the importance of integrating spatial data (i.e., DNA sequences and their associated coordinates) into macrogenetic studies, providing valuable information for future studies and conservation strategies targeting regions with high or low genetic diversity.

When inferring the evolutionary history of species and the genes they contain, the phylogenetic trees of genes can be different from those of the species and to each other, due to a variety of causes, including incomplete lineage sorting. We often wish to infer the species tree, but only reconstruct the gene trees from sequences. We then combine the gene trees to produce a species tree; methods to do this are known as summary methods, of which ASTRAL is currently among the most popular. ASTRAL has been shown to be practically accurate in many scenarios through extensive simulations. However, these simulations generally assume that the input gene trees are independent of each other. This is known to be unrealistic, as genes that are close to each other on the chromosome (or are co-evolving) have dependent phylogenies, due to the absence of unlimited recombination between the genes.

In this paper, we develop a model for generating dependent gene trees within a species tree, based on the coalescent with recombination. We then use these trees as input to ASTRAL to reassess its accuracy for dependent gene trees. Our results show that ASTRAL performs more poorly with greater dependence, both when gene trees are known and estimated from sequences. Indeed, the effect of dependence between gene trees is comparable to (if not greater than) the effect of gene tree estimation error. We then re-analyse a 37-taxon mammalian data set; under a realistic recombination rate, the estimated accuracy of ASTRAL decreases substantially (the normalised Robinson-Foulds distance increases by a factor of 4.9) relative to the accuracy previously estimated with independent gene trees, and the effective sample size for this dataset is about one-fifth of the actual sample size. This shows that the impact of gene tree dependence on the accuracy of ASTRAL (and other summary methods) can be significant.

Isolation-by-distance patterns in genetic variation are a widespread feature of the geo-graphic structure of genetic variation in many species, and many methods have been developed to illuminate such patterns in genetic data. However, long-range genetic similarities also exist, often as a result of rare or episodic long-range gene flow. Jointly characterizing patterns of isolation-by-distance and long-range genetic similarity in genetic data is an open data analysis challenge that, if resolved, could help produce more complete representations of the geographic structure of genetic data in any given species. Here, we present a computationally tractable method that identifies long-range genetic similarities in a background of spatially heterogeneous isolation-by-distance variation. The method uses a coalescent-based framework, and models long-range genetic similarity in terms of directional events with source fractions describing the fraction of ancestry at a location tracing back to a remote source. The method produces geographic maps annotated with inferred long-range edges, as well as maps of uncertainty in the geographic location of each source of long-range gene flow. We have implemented the method in a package called FEEMSmix (an extension to FEEMS from Marcus et al., 2021), and validated its implementation using simulations representative of typical data applications. We also apply this method to two empirical data sets. In a data set of over 4,000 humans (Homo sapiens) across Afro-Eurasia, we recover many known signals of long-distance dispersal from recent centuries. Similarly, in a data set of over 100 gray wolves (Canis lupus) across North America, we identify several previously unknown long-range connections, some of which were attributable to recording errors in sampling locations. Therefore, beyond identifying genuine long-range dispersals, our approach also serves as a useful tool for quality control in spatial genetic studies.

Author SummaryThe movement of individuals across landscapes shapes genetic diversity and has significant implications for both evolutionary studies and conservation efforts. Advances in sequencing now allow researchers to analyze thousands of samples from broad geographic areas, helping to estimate local gene flow. However, long-range genetic flow can occur due to a host of reasons (e.g. natural weather patterns, migration for resources, etc.), and existing methods struggle to represent these patterns. In this study, we developed a method to identify and model these long-range genetic similarities as dispersals from a source to a destination over a landscape. In applying this method to over 4,000 human samples from Afro-Eurasia, we detected signatures of known long-distance dispersals from recent centuries. In applying this method to 100 gray wolf samples from North America, we found many unexpected long-range genetic connections, some of which turned out to be recording errors in sample locations. Thus, beyond detecting real long-range dispersal, our approach also serves as a useful tool for quality control in spatial genetic studies.

BackgroundSexual selection theory is a multifaceted area of evolutionary research that has profound implications across various disciplines, including population genetics, evolutionary ecology, animal behavior, sociology, and psychology. It explores the mechanisms by which certain traits and behaviors evolve due to mate choice and competition within a species. In the context of this theory, the Jeffreys divergence measure, also known as population stability index, plays a key role in quantifying the information obtained when a deviation from random mating occurs for both discrete and continuous data. Despite the critical importance of understanding mating patterns in the context of sexual selection, there is currently no software available that can perform model selection and multimodel inference with quantitative mating data to test hypotheses about the dynamics underlying observed mating patterns. Recognizing this gap, I have developed QInfoMating which provides a comprehensive solution for analyzing and interpreting mating data within the framework of sexual selection theory.

ResultsThe program QInfoMating incorporates a user-friendly interface for performing statistical tests, best-fit model selection, and parameter estimation using multimodel inference for both discrete and continuous mating data. A use case is presented with real data of the species Echinolittorina malaccana.

ConclusionsThe application of information theory, model selection, and parameter estimation using multimodel inference are presented as powerful tools for the analysis of mating data, whether quantitative or categorical. The QInfoMating program is a tool designed to perform this type of analysis.

Conservation strategies and biodiversity assessments have long prioritized taxonomic metrics such as species richness and endemism, often neglecting intraspecific genetic diversity, a key driver of population adaptability and long-term resilience. Here, we present a scalable framework for quantifying and mapping multi-species genetic diversity using publicly available DNA sequence data. By calculating nucleotide diversity ({pi}) across taxa and aggregating values spatially, we define the Genetic Diversity Index (GDI): a site-level metric capturing geographic patterns of intraspecific genetic variation. Using simulations under different scenarios, we assessed the robustness of the GDI and implemented three corrective measures to address sampling bias and the additive effects of species richness.

We queried over 25 million accessions from public databases representing 9,409 European vascular plant species and applied this approach to [~]630,000 georeferenced sequences across 1,860 species. Our results reveal distinct genetic diversity hotspots in the Anatolian Peninsula, Southern Iberia, and Eastern Alps regions corresponding to historical glacial refugia and ecological transition zones. GDI values were largely uncorrelated with species richness or phylogenetic diversity, confirming that the index captures a unique and independent dimension of biodiversity. Our indices performed extremely well and showed that fewer than 1% of studied sites exhibited a significant effect of sampling bias, validating the methods reliability under uneven data coverage.

By integrating genetic diversity into spatial biodiversity analyses, the GDI detects large-scale patterns of evolutionary significance and fills a critical methodological gap, providing a reproducible tool to support conservation prioritization and policy at regional and global scales.

SignificanceGenetic diversity is a fundamental component of biodiversity and critical to species resilience, yet it remains absent from most biodiversity assessments. We present a scalable framework for evaluating multi-species genetic diversity across landscapes, introducing three complementary Genetic Diversity Indices (GDI) designed for different scenarios in biodiversity assessment and conservation planning. Applying this approach to European vascular plants, we reveal that genetic diversity patterns are largely decoupled from taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity, highlighting a fundamental yet overlooked dimension of biodiversity. Our framework charts a clear path for global assessments of genetic diversity in vascular plants and beyond. Incorporating GDI into conservation strategies is critical to complement traditional metrics and better safeguard evolutionary potential of biodiversity in a rapidly changing world.

The process of speciation concerns often not only pairs of species but rather groups of diverging and interacting taxa, as highlighted by recent research. Hence, to understand the evolution of species diversity and their persistence, it is crucial to understand how gene flow and evolution of reproductive isolation shape groups of closely related species. Using resequencing data, we disentangle here genomic patterns of divergence and introgression in five Formica rufa group wood ant species that are at the early stage of speciation. We first revise earlier mitochondrial phylogenies with a nuclear genomic tree, and demonstrate then introgression that is in line with observations of their current day natural hybridisation. Investigating the genome-wide differentiation and divergence we find correlations between population genetic parameters of divergence, differentiation, and diversity, that are in line with theoretical expectations for young species. Despite previously found evidence for polygenic species barriers, our data lacks the genome-wide correlation between differentiation and divergence that would be expected under a model of polygenic barriers. The likely explanation for this lack is the dominating effect of ancestral diversity at these early stages of speciation. As hybridisation has led to both deleterious and adaptive consequences within the group, we examined the signatures of introgression. We find no strong positive correlation between introgression and recombination, suggesting introgression does not have a predominantly deleterious effect. We also infer low diversity in the genomic regions with high proportions of introgression, consistent with the idea that selection has locally favoured introgression. This could be due to sharing of adaptive alleles or reduction of genetic load in the receiving species. Interestingly, gene flow in this group could potentially cross multiple species boundaries even in the absence of direct interbreeding between all the species. We discuss the long-term benefits and costs of introgression in young species, including the effect of environmental fluctuations and multi-species introgression.

Bees are vital pollinators in natural and agricultural landscapes around the globe, playing a key role in maintaining flowering plant biodiversity and ensuring food security. Among the honey bee species, the Western honey bee (Apis mellifera) is particularly significant, not only for its extensive crop pollination services but also for producing economically valuable products such as honey. Here, we analyzed whole-genome sequence data from four Apis species to explore how honey bee evolution has shaped current diversity patterns. Using Approximate Bayesian Computation, we first reconstructed the demographic history of A. mellifera in Europe, finding support for postglacial secondary contacts, therefore predating human-mediated transfers linked to modern beekeeping. However, our analysis of recent demographic changes then reveals significant bottlenecks due to beekeeping practices, which have notably affected genetic diversity. Black honey bee populations from conservatories, particularly those on islands, exhibit considerable genetic loss, raising concerns about the long-term effectiveness of current conservation strategies. Additionally, we observed a high degree of conservation in the genomic landscapes of nucleotide diversity across the four species, despite a divergence gradient spanning over 15 million years, consistent with a long-term conservation of the recombination landscapes. Taken together, our results provide the most comprehensive assessment of diversity patterns in honey bees to date and offer insights into the optimal management of resources to ensure the long-term persistence of honey bees and their invaluable pollination services.

Affordable, near-complete bacterial DNA sequencing is an indispensable analytical resource to study bacterial evolution, taxonomy, and microbial ecology. As access to high-quality DNA samples continues to improve, the combination of next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies, parallel sequencing, and large sequencing datasets to employ them can yield an uncharitable view that reference techniques and sophisticated workflows are the best tools for microbial sequencing. While NGS workflows and databases offer advantages, numerous challenges remain to accelerate microbial sequencing using these tools. To address these challenges, we introduce a workflow and pipeline framework that can benefit from NGS tools and applications. Specifically, we enable rapid identification of sequences using the robust, scalable NetBLAST approach and apply it to amplified bacterial RNA to improve sequence identity estimation (ISE) accuracy. The result is an automated, end-to-end pipeline that enables rapid (10s), unbiased, full-length identification of bacterial samples, a resource for anyone seeking rapid and accessible metagenomic-based study of microbes. Our approach uses a flexible pipeline, allowing subsequent development of custom quality or path-filtering tools to seamlessly adapt to data types. The framework is publicly available at idefal.ai and its on-demand operational support is already being deployed.

Beside its original contributions, this open-source framework serves as a powerful foundation for a range of downstream applications involving microbiome analysis and fungal genomics. For instance, the integrated workflow framework facilitates the application of multi-species DNADisc for temporal analysis of 16S rDNA abundance in environmental samples and predicts the DNA sequence of fungal isolates that do not match the reference sequence. Future development will focus on its integration with a downstream pipeline that uses enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and can discriminate pathogenic microbes from those of ecological relevance. Integrating data from the gut microbiome, and prospective applications in astrobiology are among our ambitious plans.

The incidence of infections caused by Vibrio cholerae, an etiological agent of diarrheal disease, has risen globally. Knowledge about pathogen dynamics is essential for devising effective interventions and identifying priority targets for drug development. The majority of V. cholerae biosecurity decisions rely on negative culture test results based on sequence analysis of purified DNA. Current literature relies on this approach and, in some cases, does not account for dynamics of the clone pools and genotype mixtures observed in real clinical samples. In this study, we sequenced large global gene banks from 213 positive Vibrio cholerae isolate (V. cholerae) samples isolated from patients hospitalized with cholera over the period of 2018-2022 from the WHO Global Case Definition Consortium with complete sequence data (Genome ShipWorthy Level A). We compared the diversity of paired strains using biological measurements. We also analyzed multi-variant strain and genotype/strain co-occurrence in single genome clusters. First, we established two isolation guidelines for coinfections with V. cholerae and V. Alexandrae: one for large pre-clinical divisions (Large field: 8 strains: 6 to 20), and the other for a small pre-clinical divisions (Small field: 30 strains: 6 to 24): standard culture method, not the VGP screen, and Miniaturized DNA sequencing with 10X coverage PCR (CDC genome guided). Comparative analysis of the copy number levels of each strain in the PFL and SFL fields indicates that V. cholerae and V. Alexandrae genomes tend to be polymorphic in both fields. Second, we used two different real sample ratios (F1-R:447-R and F2-R:359-R) of sequencing events to estimate their gene expression ratios. This analysis further indicated that V. cholerae has high gene expression ratios (1240-fold) across its entire genome. Third, we explored potential drug targets with V. cholerae gene data and methods from the PFL and SFL fields. We report that the type III secretion system gene (coc"CTX170, CocA) of V. cholerae was significantly overrepresented among strain and genotype co-occurrences for two to three years in the early pre-clinical division field. Specifically, this analysis suggests that there is a "hotspot" and "cold spot" in the gene set including CocA in strains with high and low co-occurrences. Importantly,

Intracellular microorganisms (bacteria) play a critical role in carbon cycling and nutrient acquisition in the oceans and both oceanic and surface ecosystems. These bacteria are distinguished by their high degree of phenotypic plasticity and wide metabolic versatility. To obtain such a large and diverse pool of microbes with multiple features, as in many biological domains, it is difficult to select which strains to include in research projects. Given the phenotypic versatility, which significantly affects the trajectory of entire bacterial populations, understanding the distribution of features is of utmost importance for establishing its reproducibility and reliability. However, the complex internal evolutionary dynamics of existing strains hinder their integration into new research projects. Here, we developed an adapted high-throughput system based on an NGS platform for screening and curation of genetically diverse genomes, called EST-eArray-Seq, and a bioinformatics pipeline that assigns genomic features to representants in experimental projects. Using both EST-eArray-Seq and the curated list of representative strains, we identified thousands of strains with exceptional microbial diversity and metabolic versatility and their features through multi-scale analysis. For instance, we discovered unique features, which we have integrated into two microbe-only models of the two main ocean communities, the bacterioplankton and the subsurface biosphere, to provide valuable knowledge and guide future research. Overall, our approach provides a network of genetically diverse genomes of known or newly characterized microorganisms. Its features are valuable for genome characterization, providing a strong knowledge base of strains with high degree of diversity and environmental resilience.

Microbiome analysis yields a large amount of diverse and unprecedented molecular data that can serve to answer fundamental questions in evolutionary biology. However, single-organism analyses can make phylogenetic inferences due to species often having similar community compositions, highlighting the need for interspecific comparisons. Here, we generate, implement, and validate an open-source, cross-kingdom framework for integrating single-organism high-throughput and single-strand-passages (SSPs) sequencing panels for protein and functional data. Specifically, we create a Python package on PyTorch for data manipulation, analysis, and rendering of high-throughput data through SGean.py, an online and open-source visualization framework. We then select several high-throughput individual-organism panel datasets, including those for 16S rRNA gene libraries and the Actinobacteria-Cynobacteria clade in the microbiota panel, to demonstrate how the framework can be utilized to conduct both broad analysis and specific single-organism analyses.

We provide application suggestions and highlight use cases of the PyTorch and GAEWrapper PyTorch Deep Learning library to accelerate the analysis of 2,964,890 per-sample individual organism high-throughput sequencing datasets. We also provide statistical results of the PKATU (Pacific Kuril Islands Tongass) dataset when tested on a subset of the Actinobacteria-Cynobacteria clade, and the appearance of an unmethylated CpG island in the lengthome panel dataset. Additionally, we describe a custom Python script to create an ANOVA with p-values within 10 or 5 microsecond delay as well as a cross-validation with an accuracy of 0.77 when using the Python and PyTorch codebase. Finally, we show the generalizability of our deep learning methodology via visualizations from paired single-organism panel-level analysis and subsequent bar-coding of samples.

In summary, we believe our framework provides a powerful tool for interspecific comparisons that is capable of parallelizing both broad and specific analysis enabling greater insights.

Despite advances in microbial diversity studies, methods for labeling and identifying microorganisms within microbial communities remain highly specific and limited to cultivable cell types. As an alternative, an approach focusing on labeled microbial barcodes utilizing ribosomal DNA (rDNA) segments with complementary sequences is being widely used for many applications, such as bacterial identification. Current computational barcode identification schemes in rRNA detect sequences from the archaeal world. Here, we aim to develop an archaeal rRNA barcode system tailored to specific bacterial representatives. To this end, we selected and revised seven core target archaeal 16S rRNA sequences to enhance their phylogenetic resolution by incorporating known archaeal phylogeny as a barcode annotation. The new barcodes were rigorously validated by performing comparative analyses with in-house assemblies of barcoded genomes from the universal genomes project pipeline. Our barcode system possesses high resolution and tight phylogenetic consensus, similar to 16S rRNA targeted sequence-based community classification systems that utilize reference strain sequences. Additionally, the new barcode system effectively identifies small, rapidly evolving bacterial taxa, including previously undetected or poorly recognized archaeal microorganisms, and accurately discriminates closely related genera. Our results highlight the potential of our barcode system to integrate taxonomically, phylogenetically, and topologically accurate microbial barcodes into community ecology, generating useful new insights to study how microbial communities are structured and how to sample such microorganisms for laboratory and environmental research.

Phylogenetic classification of bacterial pathogens takes into account the functional significance of mutations. However, most traits associated with fitness are not directly expressed, and proteins produced due to mutations are often cryptic. To improve accuracy, we characterize the coding and nontranslated features of named and native bacterial proteins. We generated a large protein database by predicting mutations for over 100,000 proteins, ranked according to predicted fitness on two bacterial hosts, Esherichia coli and Vibrio cholerae. We refined and extended a previously published method, NextStrain-Complete, that generated protein families, aiming to improve the prediction of transcribed protein signatures. We produced 78,797 protein families across 317 open domain families. Only 7,229 functional families were decoded. We refined a log-mean transposase hypothesis, implemented in NextStrain-Complete, to include any number of transcribed (but nontranslated) peptides. Our algorithm is able to correctly assign and annotate mutations in three modes: enzymatic substitutions, polymorphisms, and linkage to pathways or protein families. Finally, we assess the accuracy of various gene frequency estimators for filtering candidate proteins from protein databases and validated by bacterial genomics. A combination of large databases, especially those with abundant and easily refined sequences, is essential to build a complete reference of proteins with functional significance.

Current approaches to support complex phylogenetic analyses rely on meta-data drawn from diverse sources, which is difficult to calibrate. Therefore, a good balance between dataset quality and source heterogeneity is crucial for the development of high-performance computer models. Here, we build a nonparametric phylogenetic tree based on human molecular sequence information (HMI) using web data from gene sequences and distance matrices. Our computational method integrates a strict hierarchical (species) rule for reference-guide redundancy and a hierarchical filtering function for nonparametric scale selection. It estimates HMI on the HMI matrix and infers phylogenetic trees from HMI. Among its key features, this method proves more accurate compared to the default empirical weights in HMI and more stable across different species than other tree estimation approaches. Furthermore, the proposed method is efficient, capable of integrating existing or non-existing genomes, and fast to update HMI. We test its performance and robustness, as well as its applicability in various taxonomic contexts, in two gene clusters, bacteria and fungi. Our empirical results on the human protein functional annotations show how a multi-component method combining different software stacks can be flexible to include uncharacterized proteins.

BackgroundAnwar Usman et al. have recently shown that Cox7B protects against the Gram-negative pathogen SERRIPVX-020/AzCam by inhibiting their virulence factor Xo8 in the first study of microbiome diversity in the pathogenesis of Legionella pneumophila (Lpn) strains. ObjectiveWe aim to decipher whether the conserved conserved beta subunit of Cox7B orthologues in human disease is linked to Cox7B resistance to Salmonella Nigri. MethodsCytogenetic analyses, screening, over-expression/knockdown experiments and PCR/DNA sequencing. ResultsWe found that C826Ycox7B of human Cox7B is found in 30% of Legionella bioserotype samples, and Cox7B variants identified include the involved gene STBY9-dependent beta subunit of Cox7B. Additionally, we demonstrate that Legionella pneumophila novorsularis circumspicilorum (PLA-C1) is sensitive to C826Ycox7B-defective strains, and the drug verruconazole is also a good CQ alternative to PLA-C1. Treatment with a CQ and octanoylated-Raptor C826Ycox7B dominant negative mutant showed a dose-dependent killing (LC50 = 5.3 µM and 6.5 µM) and induction of a high recovery rate (20.2%), in addition to curing the pathogenesis-related alpha-toxin in a horse-infection model. ConclusionThus, the use of Cox7B substituted with a 5.5.5% crude-extract of human version of Cox7B could be a good workaround of the lack of resistance in common bla-CODABC-type quinolone resistant plasmids and flexible addition to a quantitative PCR-based approach for antibiotic sensitivity determination.

Model organisms have an unrivalled contribution to existing understanding of gene expression, yet also play important roles in advancing science and teaching. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has led to an unprecedented spike in human influenza viruses genome diversity. In addition to existing surveillance platforms, the pandemic sparked innovation in computational approaches to develop new and more efficient methods to monitor and quantify the dynamics of viral strains.

Here, we present OPERATE, a software library for the development of machine learning tools for the accurate and scalable calculation of clustering and molecular classification for the study of large-scale viral evolution. OPERATE was built using an open-source Python environment and has high portability for different computing platforms: Windows and Linux.

In addition to facilitating the analysis of viruses and other organismal evolutionary processes, we hope to inspire the development of new methods for broader computational genomic applications. OPERATE integrates machine learning tools with state-of-the-art software for clustering and molecular classification methods, namely MEM, SHAPE, MOMENTUM, and DISTANCE. We provide online tools and reports for the evaluation of these methods with benchmark data, and we present a comprehensive framework for processing our wide-scale datasets.

Can Mycobacterium abscessus, the soil bacterium responsible for endemic, non-endemic, and emerging actinobacillosis (Ab) infection, adapt its natural arsenal to cope with environmental stresses? Laboratory work has addressed this possibility, but there is a need for molecular biology to quantify whether features of Ab-associated natural variants are expressed under conditions known to induce Ab. We employed ultra-high-throughput quantitative (HUTQ) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to sequence PCR products, generating a broad target size of 200 to 800 base pairs. Ninety-five of the 200-base pair primers, measuring a total of 109,384 reads, were subjected to comparative analysis by positional cloning. This analysis identified two unique structural features that distinguish M. abscessus from uninfected pure cultures. Sequencing of three additional representative isolates showed the following: (1) Use of operon 17A (durae operon 17A) rather than 24E (eumcrinic operon 17A) is sufficient for induction of Ab-associated Ab PCR. Furthermore, operon 17B (dsma operon 17A) is not necessary for the expression of known P5 (pMN-P5) and P4 (P5-P4) sequences in M. abscessus. (2) a sub-unit of P5, d3-DnaH, linked to such P5, was positively selected using random barcode sequencing and genome wide comparative analysis. (3) Overall, this analysis suggests that the novel P5 protein identified in Ab infected mycobacteria contains a P2 domain and an internal kinase domain.

Phylogenomic analyses of a global dataset of isolates categorised as human, animal, plant, or environmental strains suggest that K.var are broadly disseminated regardless of hosts or habitats and exhibit genomic variability that is relevant for occupying and transmitting within and across multiple sources. Ancestral state analyses confirm that K.var are originally derived from non-human sources. Genome-wide association analyses of human versus non-human isolates of K.var indicate isolates from human origins are linked to the loss of cold-shock response genes such as lpxP and cspB. Importantly, human K.var isolates also showed enriched antimicrobial resistance gene content and diversity acquired through mobile genetic elements, horizontal gene transfer and mutations within the chromosomal loci which underscore the impact of antimicrobial exposure and proximity to antibiotic resistant K.pne in nosocomial environments. Capsular profiles of K.var suggest high levels of variability in gene composition and indicate that gene functionality for wcaJ in capsule formation differs between K.var and K.pne. Although capsular specialisation was not observed in a host/habitat or lineage-dependent manner, human isolates harbour, on average, a higher siderophore gene content in addition to mrkD mutations which impact on fimbriae and biofilm formation. There is limited evidence of any specific K.var lineages exhibiting convergence of both virulence and antimicrobial resistance genotypes which suggest that these attributes are evolving independently in clinical strains. Our work highlights that gene attrition and acquisition provide a basis for adaptation of K.var as human pathogens. The broad distribution and evolution of K.var highlight the need for improved diagnostic precision and surveillance under a One Health framework.

Approximately 10% of all bacterial genomes sequenced thus far contain a secondary replicon. This property of bacterial populations vastly increases genomic diversity within phylogenetically narrow groups. Members of the genus Variovorax have extensive heterogeneity in genome architecture, including sequenced isolates containing plasmids, megaplasmids, and chromids. Many of the Variovorax genomes in the NCBI database were generated using only short-read data and were assembled to the permanent draft stage. We acquired a set of these isolates and used the MinION long-read sequencing device to generate additional data to allow hybrid assemblies of these genomes. Here we present the finished assemblies of 15 Variovorax isolates from diverse ecosystems that were previously only available as permanent drafts. When added to the previously published Variovorax assemblies for EPS, CSUSB, and VAI-C and those published by other groups, we found significant diversity in genome architecture. We found that there are plasmids, megaplasmids, and chromids that are distinguishable using Guanine-Cytosine (G+C content) content as a signal. We identified a plasmid integration event in NFACC27 and identify potential evolutionary relationships in the second replicons based on ParB homology as well as ANI. The evidence suggests that Variovorax is like its sister taxon Burkholderia, highly capable of acquiring and maintaining stable secondary replicons. The plasticity of these architectures and the mechanisms for maintenance remain a topic for future research.

MotivationOver the past decades, genome databases have expanded exponentially, often incorporating highly similar genomes at the same taxonomic level. This redundancy can hinder taxonomic classification, leading to difficulties distinguishing between closely related sequences and increasing computational demands. While some novel taxonomic classification tools address this redundancy by filtering the input genome database, there is limited work exploring the impact of different sequence dereplication methods across taxonomic classification tools.

ResultsWe assess the effect of genome selection approaches on taxonomic classification using both bacterial and viral datasets. Our results demonstrate that careful selection of reference genomes can improve classification accuracy. We also show that using prior knowledge about a metagenomic sample, such as sampling location, can significantly improve classification accuracy. Finally, we find that using a redundancy-filtered genome database generally reduces the computational resources required, with minimal loss in classification accuracy.

The SARS-CoV-2 genome occupies a unique place in infection biology - it is the most highly sequenced genome on earth (making up over 20% of public sequencing datasets) with fine scale information on sampling date and geography, and has been subject to unprecedented intense analysis. As a result, these phylogenetic data are an incredibly valuable resource for science and public health. However, the vast majority of the data was sequenced by tiling amplicons across the full genome, with amplicon schemes that changed over the pandemic as mutations in the viral genome interacted with primer binding sites. In combination with the disparate set of genome assembly workflows and lack of consistent quality control (QC) processes, the current genomes have many systematic errors that have evolved with the virus and amplicon schemes. These errors have significant impacts on the phylogeny, and therefore over the last few years, many thousands of hours of researchers time has been spent in "eyeballing" trees, looking for artefacts, and then patching the tree.

Given the huge value of this dataset, we therefore set out to reprocess the complete set of public raw sequence data in a rigorous amplicon-aware manner, and build a cleaner phylogeny. Here we provide a global tree of 4,471,579 samples, built from a consistently assembled set of high quality consensus sequences from all available public data as of June 2024, viewable at https://viridian.taxonium.org. Each genome was constructed using a novel assembly tool called Viridian (https://github.com/iqbal-lab-org/viridian), developed specifically to process amplicon sequence data, eliminating artefactual errors and mask the genome at low quality positions. We provide simulation and empirical validation of the methodology, and quantify the improvement in the phylogeny. We hope the tree, consensus sequences and Viridian will be a valuable resource for researchers.

BackgroundGenomic surveillance is extensively used for tracking public health outbreaks and healthcare-associated pathogens. Despite advancements in bioinformatics pipelines, there are still significant challenges in terms of infrastructure, expertise, and security when it comes to continuous surveillance. The existing pipelines often require the user to set up and manage their own infrastructure and are not designed for continuous surveillance that demands integration of new and regularly generated sequencing data with previous analyses. Additionally, academic projects often do not meet the privacy requirements of healthcare providers.

ResultsWe present Solu, a cloud-based platform that integrates genomic data into a real-time, privacy-focused surveillance system.

EvaluationSolus accuracy for taxonomy assignment, antimicrobial resistance genes, and phylogenetics, was comparable to established pathogen surveillance pipelines. In some cases, Solu identified antimicrobial resistance genes that were previously undetected. Together, these findings demonstrate the efficacy of our platform.

ConclusionsBy enabling reliable, user-friendly, and privacy-focused genomic surveillance, Solu has the potential to bridge the gap between cutting-edge research and practical, widespread application in healthcare settings. The platform is available for free academic use at platform.solugenomics.com.

Type 11 secretion systems (T11SS) are broadly distributed among proteobacteria, with more than 3000 T11SS family outer membrane proteins (OMPs) comprising 10 major sequence similarity network (SSN) clusters. Of these, only 7, all from animal-associated cluster 1, have been experimentally verified as secretins of cargo, including adhesins, hemophores, and metal binding proteins. To identify novel cargo of a more diverse set of T11SS, we identified gene families co-occurring in gene neighborhoods with either cluster 1 or marine microbe-associated cluster 3 T11SS OMP genes. We developed bioinformatic controls to ensure perceived co-occurrences are specific to T11SS, and not general to OMPs. We found that both cluster 1 and cluster 3 T11SS OMPs frequently co-occur with single carbon metabolism and nucleotide synthesis pathways, but that only cluster 1 T11SS OMPs had significant co-occurrence with metal and heme pathways, as well as with mobile genetic islands, potentially indicating diversified function of this cluster. Cluster 1 T11SS co-occurrences included 2556 predicted cargo proteins, unified by the presence of a C-terminal {beta}-barrel domain, which fall into 141 predicted UniRef50 clusters and approximately 10 different architectures: 4 similar to known cargo and 6 uncharacterized types. We experimentally demonstrate T11SS-dependent secretion of an uncharacterized cargo type with homology to Plasmin sensitive protein (Pls). Unexpectedly, genes encoding marine cluster 3 T11SS OMPs only rarely co-occurred with the C-terminal {beta}-barrel domain and instead frequently co-occurred with DUF1194-containing genes. Overall, our results show that with sufficiently large-scale and controlled genomic data, T11SS-dependent cargo proteins can be accurately predicted.

Impact StatementWe describe a novel method for controlling genomic neighborhood analyses and use this controlled co-occurrence technique to examine two distinct clusters of genes from the recently described type 11 secretion system (T11SS): Cluster 1, predominantly encoded by host-associated microbes and Cluster 3, encoded by marine microbes. We found that both clusters of predicted T11SS frequently co-occur with single carbon metabolism and nucleotide synthesis pathways, but only the host-associated cluster co-occurred with iron uptake pathways. Using these datasets, we predicted 2687 T11SS dependent cargo with approximately ten unique architectures, six of which have not previously been linked to T11SS. Finally, we validate our results by demonstrating T11SS-dependent secretion of a cargo protein with one of the novel architectures, plasmin-sensitive surface protein Pls from Haemophilus parahaemolyticus.

Data SummaryThis paper describes genomic co-occurrences of T11SS OMP sequences originally identified through sequence similarity networking in a previous publication [3] as constituents of similarity clusters, 1 and 3. Accession IDs and assorted metadata for those clusters/networks are listed in Table S1 of that article: https://journals.asm.org/doi/suppl/10.1128/mbio.01956-21/suppl_file/mbio.01956-21-st001.xlsx. All other supporting data, accession IDs, code, and protocols have been provided within this article or through supplementary data files. Additionally, all supplemental data are available on Figshare (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28514069.v2) [1].

The identification of succinct, universal fingerprints that enable the characterization of individual taxonomies can reveal insights into trait development and can have widespread applications in pathogen diagnostics, human healthcare, ecology and the characterization of biomes. Here, we investigated the existence of peptide k-mer sequences that are exclusively present in a specific taxonomy and absent in every other taxonomic level, termed taxonomic quasi-primes. By analyzing proteomes across 24,073 species, we identified quasi-prime peptides specific to superkingdoms, kingdoms, and phyla, uncovering their taxonomic distributions and functional relevance. These peptides exhibit remarkable sequence uniqueness at six- and seven-amino- acid lengths, offering insights into evolutionary divergence and lineage-specific adaptations. Moreover, we show that human quasi-prime loci are more prone to harboring pathogenic variants, underscoring their functional significance. This study introduces taxonomic quasi-primes and offers insights into their contributions to proteomic diversity, evolutionary pathways, and functional adaptations across the tree of life, while emphasizing their potential impact on human health and disease.

Mycobacterium abscessus is a rapidly growing non-tuberculosis mycobacterium that opportunistically causes pulmonary infections and is notable for its high resistance to antibiotics. While ubiquitous in environmental reservoirs such as soil, water, and biofilms, the genetic factors that enable certain strains to invade and persist in human hosts have remained elusive. To address this gap, we compared whole-genome sequences from 45 environmental isolates-- primarily collected on Hawaii Island--with a globally sourced set of clinical isolates retrieved from NCBI RefSeq. Our phylogenetic reconstruction delineated environmental and clinical lineages, and pangenome profiling revealed a conserved core genome of approximately 4,800 genes alongside a large accessory genome. Crucially, we found 20 genes conserved in clinical isolates, but not environmental isolates. Clinical isolates were found to have conserved genes coding for erm(41), three transcriptional regulators, a pilus synthesis gene, an NADP-dependent oxidoreductase, a carbonic anhydrase, a probable L-ectoine synthase, a ribonuclease P protein component, and 11 hypothetical genes, whereas environmental isolated did not conserve any of these genes. This indicates that clinical isolates have undergone broad changes relating to metabolism, pilus biosynthesis, and transcriptional regulators, which may be necessary for pathogenicity. The candidate virulence markers uncovered here lay the groundwork for experimental validation, rapid diagnostics for non-tuberculous mycobacteria, and targeted surveillance of environmental reservoirs to mitigate the emergence of clinically significant strains.

ImportanceMycobacterium abscessus is an emerging pathogen that causes pulmonary infections in susceptible individuals. Though currently an opportunistic pathogen, M. abscessus may be undergoing evolutionary changes to become an obligate pathogen. Because of this, there is the need to identify markers of virulence in M. abscessus in order to better screen isolates and assess their risk of causing infection. This also provides the opportunity to study a similar pathogenesis to what Mycobacterium tuberculosis may have undergone. This study revealed that clinical isolates of M. abscessus have conserved genes relating to pilus biosynthesis, metabolism, and transcriptional regulators that environmental isolates do not have. These conserved genes may be required for M. abscessus to acquire virulence, and these genes have potential use as biomarkers to screen isolates for possible pathogenicity.

Huge phages are remarkable for their expansive genomes ([≥]200 kbp, and up to 841 kbp to date), global distribution, and intricate functional repertoires. However, their study has been hindered by challenges in genome identification and the lack of a comprehensive reference database. Using vRep, we established the Huge Phage Genome Collection (HPGC), a curated resource of 7,295 non-redundant huge phage genomes spanning 4,613 species-level groups. Within HPGC, we identified an overlooked and prevalent clade, HP8026, which constitutes ~1.2% of human gut metagenomic reads, suggesting its potential in fecal contamination monitoring and a promissing modulator of gut microbiome dynamics. Complementing HPGC, we developed the Huge Phage Protein Structure Database (HPDB), which catalogs 15,594 structure clusters derived from 589,960 predicted proteomes. Notably, 40% of these clusters presented in huge phages only, exhibit specific protein folds. Additionally, 3% of the HPDB clusters were absent in other viral forms, including the plasmid-originated ArdC that could protect huge phages from the antiviral mechanisms of their hosts. Collectively, HPGC and HPDB provide a pioneering framework for exploring the evolution, functional innovation, and biotechnological potential of huge phages, while serving as indispensable references for viral ecology and structural biology.

A novel bacteriophage vB_CoeS_P1, isolated in the surface waters of the Cochin estuary of Kerala, India, was identified as the first phage known to infect Vibrio hepatarius. Transmission electron microscopy analysis revealed that the phage had a myovirus morphotype with an icosahedral head and a long contractile tail. Characterization experiments show that the phage was stable across a temperature range of 4{degrees}C to 60{degrees}C, a pH of 4 to 12, and a salinity range of 0.5 % to 16%. One-step growth curve analysis revealed a burst size of 30 PFU/Cell and a latent period of 20 minutes. The phage contains a double-stranded DNA with 136,927 bp and 34.93% GC content. The NCBI Blastn analysis reveals that vB_CoeS_P1 exhibits very low sequence similarity (1% query coverage and 77.82% identity) with Vb_VpaM_R16F (OP793884.1). It has 265 predicted ORFs, among them 57 have putative functions with no tRNA, antibiotic encoding genes, and resistance encoding genes. Three putative auxiliary metabolic genes were identified, encoding pyrophosphohydrolase enzyme (ORF 75), PhoH-like phosphate starvation-inducible (ORF 34), and Endonuclease V N-glycosylase UV repair enzyme (ORF 248). Phylogenetic analysis of conversed genes revealed that vB_CoeS_P1 is clustered with Vb_VpaM_R16F but diverged into a distinct clade. Further whole genome proteomic tree analysis, comparative genome analysis using average nucleotide identity (ANI), and network analysis confirmed that vB_CoeS_P1 contains a unique genetic and evolutionary architecture. These findings support the proposal of a new bacteriophage family Estovirdae, within the Caudoviricetes class.

sample_q_texts: The classic property of protein aggregates of flexibility and reversibility highlights the critical role of their periodicity, the long-range spatial network of hydrophobic amino acid residues that surround each protein monomer. However, it remains uncertain how much periodicity strongly influences the functional properties of dimers. Although structural property volume changes are crucial in determining physiological function, using the high-resolution structure of one particular dimer, A24, we show that protein periodic volume changes are minimally linked to aggregate turnover, and two large structural changes within a dimer are sufficient to abolish dimer function. We show that even short-range structural perturbations of the repeat along these positions, first discovered in the fold of the dimer in 2018, drive an association-maintenance coexistence-disassociation behavior in the two monomers at each repeat position and limit a reversible free monomeric form. This coexistence behavior in a similar dimer molecule predicts a molecular magnitude where it is likely that in turn mediating reversible association and disassembly via reactive monomer-transient bonding. For the 2D model, these factors determine the prevalence of disordered binding rather than structural cooperativity in the free monomer and determine the extent of association-disassociation-free coexistence. The stability of free monomeric and transiently bound 2D dimers is broadly insensitive to perturbation of the specific dimer structure.

Extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins are highly conserved and often have poorly defined domains for structure, ligand binding and biomineralization. Previously-discovered solubilization buffers and/or oligomerization reagents have inspired selective inhibition of PPIases to provide improved spatial resolution and accessibility for binding studies and solutions for probing non-native protein conformational dynamics. While detergents have the advantage of easily dissolving proteins and increasing accessibility for purification, their concentrations are typically low, they only solve protein secondary structures, and the induced conformational changes are often either too small or/and unstable to study. Our studies aimed to measure and detect forces involved in large domain-recognition complexes through the development of the new bimolecular scaffold sterically stabilized ensemble (bb-SS-ES) via relaxation inhibition with difference in molecular flux. We here systematically detect PPIase interaction by chemical inhibition in membranes to study specific interactions through a molecular dynamics simulation. We further show how the receptor rigidizes the dis/magnetized ECM-coiled protein to study complex-specific interactions while measuring the PPIase-induced change in DP and DB using a small-angle X-ray scattering angle (PACSO-XS-ASR) method. This showed that the PPIase interaction prevents maturation of the substrate interface without leading to structural disruption, thereby allowing binding of specificity-designed motifs. The results of this study advance model systems that can potentially detect interactions between biochemical constructs and machine learning as a means to enable molecular dissection of cell-matrix interactions to gain insight into the mechanisms of disease, drug development, or cancer.

Protein folding is a central process governing the fidelity of biochemical reactions. Proteins control the high-level stability of biochemical processes and must be able to cope with a broad range of conditions. Inosine diphosphate (IdP) is the universal key that pairs with a single amino acid to form native misfolded-protein (MPI) substrates. These formed IDP-amino acids span a unique dynamic range of structure to give them maximum flexibility with other biochemical intermediates. In this study, we determined structural and thermodynamic properties of native and apo-IdP (nearly identical to apo-GDP) at a variety of temperatures, pH, and buffer composition. We used the Cryo-TEM attachment protocol to record several numerous protein conformations from apo-IdP and apo-GDP solution. Our structures reveal the relative roles of ion pair dissociation, anti-parallel string folding and protein contact interactions, and reveal favorable orientations to facilitate mixing of protein phases. Our results demonstrate that apo-IdP remains stable at room temperature with similar stability to apo-GDP at temperatures >60°C and near room temperature. We propose a new model that describes the conformational dynamics of GPI-C bond forming -i.e., protein-protein interaction, combined with the thermodynamic consequences of open and closed channels.

Liquid water present at low temperatures, under atmospheric pressure, is thought to be the starting point of protein folding. A key insight in this sequence process is that the protein monomer can adopt complex structures that prevent access for hydrophobic environments, providing sufficient energy for more metastable folding states in liquid water. Here, we reveal a key determinant that subverts this structure-stabilizing strategy: the ubiquitous, global disturbance in the water temperature. Our experiments provide the first molecular and thermodynamic mechanistic insights into how the temperature, as well as solute composition, affects the β-sheet-forming/amyloid-forming transition (SMT) point. We show that the conformational landscape of the hydration-directed head formed by water tension alters the locus of the SMT transition, instead placing it on a higher surface temperature, relative to the head that would result in the observed SMT transition. Importantly, these results clearly demonstrate that the SMT transitions are regulated by temperature alone, without requiring an increase in the solute concentration. Our study provides molecular insights into the protein folding mechanism, a first-principles principle from a fundamental perspective, which in turn motivates mechanistic studies to design such protocols for different conformations, as well as the design of organofunctional protein-based devices for biomedical applications.

Protein complexes employ a variety of molecular recognition elements to serve a range of roles in biology. Individual scaffolds operate in concert to recognize specific targets with extraordinary specificity and agility. Recognition motifs containing a folding block like loops and bends are especially advantageous and frequently serve as structural elements. Biomacromolecular components employed to bind a target include globular protein motifs with motifs composed of sidechains capable of affinity-stabilization by cooperative binding to the scaffold. This highlights the presence of molecular recognition elements that modulate interactions between protein scaffold homologs. Ligand proteins are especially advantageous where the scaffold homologs lack homologous amino acid identities. Structural basis of hydrophobic interaction module is present in the influenza A virus nucleocapsid protein (N protein) only due to selective, precise, but labile interaction with the loop in the NP2 domain, which likely facilitated rapid uptake of the N protein via a sequence-specific interaction with the NP2 domain. Ab initio generation of allosteric interactions is also driven by competition to recognize a specific target to enhance function. Functional validation of dual-RNA assist during replication-coupled transcription facilitated by nucleosome-bound promoters is supported by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, NMR spectroscopy and high-throughput screening experiments. Probing the role of protein scaffolds in COVID-19 N protein requires a different approach. An engineered pathogen-selectable serine antibody oligonucleotide scaffold reveals unexpected reactivity to the wild type of the N protein within its C-terminus, consistent with an amino-terminal sequestration of the C-terminus of the N protein in the nucleus. This offers opportunity to probe an essential structural element of the N protein where the C-terminal amino acid sequence is conserved in the divergent region of the virus.

Large therapeutic proteins must often fold in the absence of their protein partners. Despite the great success of many soluble recombinant proteins, the folding process is still insufficiently understood. The freezing experiment is often used to investigate the water-water interface and the folding patterns of such proteins. However, the often-taken point of view is the side-coordinate views, which are in the absence of a static protein-enzyme solution. Here, we use an intra-coordinative point of view to study the phase behavior of such proteins. The isothermal creep curves are recorded under a constant pressure or a varying pressure that are applied to the samples in either a single stage or in a single fold. The multilinear calibration describes the relation between the curves and the hydrostatic pressure. A comparative analysis of the threefold and the cubic model shows that the third order Bethe-Petersen model, as the conjugate bethelayer, describes the relationship with superior accuracy compared to the discrete gamma-Bethe-Petersen and the cubic model.

Protein misfolding, especially of structural proteins, induces irreversible disaggregation, which plays an important role in pathogenesis and longevity of cell. However, the existence of misfolded proteins in cells is unknown. Because the virus has a highly stable or stabilized form, how SARS-CoV-2 N protein disassembles was puzzling. This research showed that the N-terminal peptide fragment of SARS-CoV-2 N protein undergoes supramolecular association in the pentameric phase through certain surface properties of N-terminal peptide. These surface properties (superstitious interactions) endow super-stable and stable N-term peptide with advantages in both intracellular and extracellular environments. The interaction of SARS-CoV-2 N-term peptide with cellular surface proteins and the viral lipid membrane is modified. Among them, the interaction with the co-operative endonuclease F3 domain of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) cleavage-related protein (Dcr) is key. The detection of the RAGE-binding site on super-stable N-term peptide reveals that the super-stable N-term peptide is the only inhibitor of RAGE. In addition, the detection of the quadruple proteasome inhibitors, which is believed to be the most likely target site for N-terminal peptide, discovered that SARS-CoV-2 N-terminal peptide was unlikely to bind directly with proteasome inhibitor Dpe1-L474I. These results help explain why N-term peptide has the highest binding affinity with super-stable N-term peptide but has the lowest affinity with N-terminal non-stable peptide. These findings suggest a function for the super-stable N-term peptide as a substrate, enhancing the stability of N-terminal peptide and the conformational flexibility of N-term peptide. This highlights the universality of the structural integrity of N-terminal peptides and provides a new insight into the COVID-19 virus infection process.

The insertion of hydrophobic or polar residues between cysteine-rich globular proteins can commonly increase stability by providing an electronegative charge (e.g., anionic or basic residues) or hydrophobic scaffold that prevents protein aggregation in the apolar phase. However, in non-cell-based kinetic studies, relying on hydrophobicity-induced aggregation-induced changes of folding pattern for predicting the impact of hydrophobic residues on stability could yield substantial deviations to real-life observations. Here, a multiscale and multiapproach computational approach, called intraprotein NMR-map (iProMap), was developed to predict relative stability of hydrophobically incorporated or intrinsically disordered (iD) residues, mainly based on biochemical kinetic models describing peptide secondary structural changes or fold changes, and the solvent accessible surfaces of the corresponding stacking partners. iProMap computed the propensity of a given hydrophobic residue to adopt 71 stable fold assignments in every 40 amino acid residues surrounding the residue in the bulk of the protein. The overall stability prediction is based on least squares regression analysis based on the eFold1200 model and thus independent of amino acid sequence bias. Simulation results based on these predictions demonstrated that intrinsically disordered residues or hydrophobic residues adopt lower stability, especially in β-rich and aromatic regions. In particular, these residues have significant cryo- or ortho-deprotons, leading to increased stability compared to stable folding models.

Protein folding is a highly regulated process, influenced by a small number of hydrophobic amino acid residues that interact through dynamic hydrogen bonds. The fibril assembly that links these highly ordered protein structures into extended proteins are mediated by highly organized hydrophobic domain structures in F-actin, endomembrane membranes, and secretory vesicles. Local detergent affinity induces the formation of planar zones, that are sequentially gated into closed conformations, and facilitate filament assembly by multiple interactions between protein strands. To study the mechanism of fibril assembly, we report the identification of the kinetic drivers and the co-factor critical role of F-actin as a force-freeer that binds to the polarization of the protein domain. Our work demonstrates the highly ordered architecture of F-actin towards its anchoring-dependent kinetics at these critical sites in the fibril-assembly process, driving dynamic interactions that can guide the conformation and concentration of F-actin molecules to interact with membrane domains and the sequence-specific F-actin binding sites in the surrounding cytoplasmic membrane. This proposal reveals a complex mechanism driving membrane-driven nucleation of the fibrillar domain that is important for the assembly of many microbial membrane-associated structures and serves as a model to study the assembly process and modulation of mammalian mRNA binding proteins.

Synthetic amyloid fibrillation driven by interactions between non-proteinogenic amino acids is a long-standing research focus. However, under the same experimental conditions, natural amyloid fibrils have discrete fractions of fibrillar monomers with different morphologies. This dichotomy presents a challenge to model amyloid fibril structure from a monomodal fibril population. In this study, we investigate the effects of monomer morphologies and monomer ratios on fibrillation processing in recombinant systems, aiming to address the issue of fibril morphology influence on fibrillation properties with an emphasis on the fibril size and monomer incorporation along fibril lengths, insights into fibril morphology impact on structure-property relationships, and further direction for fibrillar structures in a pathological context. Our models are based on the composition of disordered alpha-helix in aqueous microfluidic channels and allow us to predict fibril morphologies based on composition alone, with each monomer morphology represented by a superposition of molecular dynamics simulations. We show that microfluidic channels with small radii allow large fibril monomers to be excluded from their native microenvironments, and so serve as the precursor to fibril aggregation and fibril structure. We interpret this phenomenon as a result of fibril conformations induced by <italic>Trp</italic>-driven intramolecular motions within the hydrophobic cavity of microfluidic channels. We demonstrate that the properties of fibrillar monomers within a surface-interacting microfluidic channel are determined by the arrangement and composition of the monomers (2D fibril structure, number, length) rather than by surface charges or curvature, and we can improve our understanding of structure-property relationships by providing a model using synthetic microfluidic channels that are <italic>tr</italic>-substituted.
Investigative QuestionHow can we explain the observed functional diversity of amyloid-fibrils and control fibrillation resolution for design-to-safety studies?
Synoptic QuestionsHow do fibril-facing kinetics affect fibril macro-scale structure-property relationships?
Thesis ClassificationMicroscopical biological techniques and methods, Tools, Processes, Materials, Results, Protocols
