sample_p_texts: Integral membrane proteins carry out essential functions in the cell, and their activities are often modulated by specific protein-lipid interactions in the membrane. Here, we elucidate the intricate role of cardiolipin (CDL), a regulatory lipid, as a stabilizer of membrane proteins and their complexes. Using the in silico-designed model protein TMHC4_R (ROCKET) as a scaffold, we employ a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and native mass spectrometry to explore the protein features that facilitate preferential lipid interactions and mediate stabilization. We find that the spatial arrangement of positively charged residues as well as local conformational flexibility are factors that distinguish stabilizing from non-stabilizing CDL interactions. However, we also find that even in this controlled, artificial system, a clear-cut distinction between binding and stabilization is difficult to attain, revealing that overlapping lipid contacts can partially compensate for the effects of binding site mutations. Extending our insights to naturally occurring proteins, we identify a stabilizing CDL site within the E. coli rhomboid intramembrane protease GlpG and uncover its regulatory influence on enzyme substrate preference. In this work, we This work establishes a framework for engineering functional lipid interactions, paving the way for the design of proteins with membrane-specific properties or functions.

Insulins structural adaptations have been extensively studied at neutral and basic pH; however, the effects of water and anion coordination on allosteric regions under various acidic conditions remain unexplored. Given the critical role of polar interactions in allosteric modulation, investigating structured water movements across extended pH intervals is essential for understanding solvent-mediated stabilization mechanisms in the monomer form of insulin. Structures of acid-stable cubic insulin crystals were determined in the divalent anionic form of citric acid solutions over a pH range of 2 to 6 to investigate the effects of water and anion coordination, along with charge distribution, on protein conformation. Synchrotron X-ray diffraction data were collected at resolutions ranging from 1.4 to 1.76 [A], with refined models exhibiting R-factors between 0.19 and 0.21. While the spatial arrangement of most proteins is highly conserved, [~]90% of the water coordination network and polar interactions alter local residue motion and intrinsic dynamics of the structures as the pH is changed. This is in line with previously determined structures at pH 7-11, allowing for a comprehensive structural analysis in the pH range of pH 2-11. Three key observations emerged: (i) water coordinations undergo a prominent shift toward the isoelectric point of insulin (pH 5-7), (ii) water molecules and anions function as allosteric modulators to stabilize the T-state of insulin at the pH range 2 to 6, and (iii) at extreme pH values 2 and 11, increased solubility correlates with the structural adoption of insulins most active form, wherein hydration within the allosteric pocket supports monomer stabilization in the T-state. Combined with the computational analyses, pH-dependent electrostatic redistributions primarily affect side-chain dynamics and local protein motion. This solvent-coupled allosteric regulation provides a mechanistic framework for solvent-mediated protein stabilization, offering a novel insight into the rational design of insulin formulations through controlled protonation and hydration strategies.

Structures using X-ray diffraction data collected to 2.3 [A], 2.85 [A], and 2.88 [A] resolutions have been determined for the long-acting dihexamer insulin at three different temperatures ranging from 100{degrees}K to 300{degrees}K. It is determined that the unit-cell value of insulin crystal at 100{degrees}K temperature has changed at 200{degrees}K temperature. This change might be due primarily to subtle repacking of the molecule and loss of noncovalent interactions of myristic acid that binds two hexamers, exhibiting the largest movements. Computational analyses show that allosteric residues and fatty-acid binding residue of insulin hexamers display reduced overall collectivity and inter-residue coupling, likely arising from crystal mosaicity increase and structural fluctuations through elevated thermal motion. This breakpoint has been observed at a characteristic temperature of 200{degrees}K, perhaps emphasizing underlying alterations in the dynamic structure of the fatty acid-solvent interface in dimer of hexamer. Combined with computational analysis, findings reveal key insights into thermal stability mechanisms crucial for developing thermostable insulin formulations in industrial applications.

TeaserTemperature-driven shifts in insulins structure reveal dynamic changes crucial for enhancing thermal stability in drug formulations.

How motions in enzymes might be linked to catalytic function is of considerable general interest. Advances in X-ray crystallography and cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) offer the promise of elucidating functionally relevant conformational changes that are not easily studied by other biophysical methods. Here we use 3D variability analysis (3DVA) of the cryo-EM map for wild-type (WT) human asparagine synthetase (ASNS) to identify a functional role for the Arg-142 side chain as a gate that mediates ammonia access to a catalytically relevant intramolecular tunnel. Our 3DVA-derived hypothesis is assessed experimentally, using the R142I variant in which Arg-142 is replaced by isoleucine, and by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on independent, computational models of the WT human ASNS monomer and its catalytically relevant, ternary complex with {beta}-aspartyl-AMP and MgPPi. Residue fluctuations in the MD trajectories for the human ASNS monomer are consistent with those determined for 3DVA-derived structures. These MD simulations also indicate that the gating function of Arg-142 is separate from the molecular events that form a continuous tunnel linking the two active sites. Experimental support for Arg-142 playing a role in intramolecular ammonia translocation is provided by the glutamine-dependent synthetase activity of the R142 variant relative to WT ASNS. MD simulations of computational models for the R142I variant and the R142I/{beta}-aspartyl-AMP/MgPPi ternary complex provide a possible molecular basis for this observation. Overall, the combination of 3DVA with MD simulations is a generally applicable approach to generate testable hypotheses of how conformational changes in buried side chains might regulate function in enzymes.

Emerging evidence suggests that amino acid homorepeats (HRs) in proteins (HRPs) contribute to protein interactability. What is the role of HRs in human-pathogen protein interactions? We find that pathogens engage physiologically important human HRPs, thereby affecting diverse host physiological processes. From the pathogen standpoint, (i) eukaryotic pathogens engage more HRPs but with host-sparse HRs, leading to disparate and discriminate interactions, (ii) prokaryotic pathogens engage less HRPs but with host-abundant non-polar HRs via host protein proxies bringing about discriminate or promiscuous interactions and (iii) viral pathogens engage more HRPs with host-abundant polar uncharged HRs affecting promiscuous interactions using host-partner HR tract mimicry. To propel further research, we introduce a resource Hi-PHI (http://hiphi.iisertirupati.ac.in/) cataloging critical information about human and pathogen HRPs and HRs. We propose mechanisms to (i) repurpose drugs targeting human HRPs engaged by pathogens for treating different infections and (ii) exploit HRs and their flanks as targets for pathogen-targeted anti-infectives.

Cellular desiccation - the loss of nearly all water from the cell - is a recurring stress in an increasing number of ecosystems that can drive protein unfolding and aggregation. For cells to survive, at least some of the proteome must resume function upon rehydration. Which proteins tolerate desiccation, and the molecular determinants that underlie this tolerance, are largely unknown. Here, we apply quantitative and structural proteomic mass spectrometry to show that certain proteins possess an innate capacity to tolerate rehydration following extreme water loss. Structural analysis points to protein surface chemistry as a key determinant for desiccation tolerance, which we test by showing that rational surface mutants can convert a desiccation sensitive protein into a tolerant one. Desiccation tolerance also has strong overlap with cellular function, with highly tolerant proteins responsible for production of small molecule building blocks, and intolerant proteins involved in energy-consuming processes such as ribosome biogenesis. As a result, the rehydrated proteome is preferentially enriched with metabolite and small molecule producers and depleted of some of the cells heaviest consumers. We propose this functional bias enables cells to kickstart their metabolism and promote cell survival following desiccation and rehydration.

TeaserProteins can resist extreme dryness by tuning the amino acids on their surfaces.

Given the repetitive structure of crystalline ice, its unsurprising that highly active ice-binding proteins, often with beta-roll structures, also have repeating motifs. Here, we introduce a de novo designed family of ice-binding twistless alpha-helical repeat (iTHR) proteins. Each iTHR protein comprises two planar layers of parallel alpha-helices connected by loops--a structural topology not seen in native ice-binding proteins. The ice-binding helices feature an ordered array of TXXXAXXXAXX motifs, spaced to match the pyramidal {201} and secondary prism plane {110} ice lattice facets, and engineered with a 98.2{degrees} turn angle per residue to orient threonines uniformly towards the ice surface. iTHR proteins show high solubility, thermostability, and produce varied ice crystal morphologies depending on their intended target facet. Crucially, iTHRs exhibit ice recrystallization inhibition (IRI) at critical concentrations comparable to those of many native globular ice-binding proteins. Extensive site-specific mutagenesis shows that ice-binding activity in iTHR proteins is robust, remaining largely unaffected by changes in chemical composition. Variation in the repeat number reveals a non-monotonic relationship to IRI activity. X-ray crystal structures of two designs confirm the intended orientation of threonines, uniformly pointing toward the ice surface. The iTHR family provides a versatile platform to systematically investigate the complex structure-activity relationships underlying protein-ice interactions.

Angiotensin-I converting enzyme (ACE) regulates the levels of disparate bioactive peptides, notably converting angiotensin-I to angiotensin-II and degrading amyloid beta. ACE is a heavily glycosylated dimer, containing 4 analogous catalytic sites, and exists in membrane bound and soluble (sACE) forms. ACE inhibition is a frontline, FDA-approved, therapy for cardiovascular diseases yet is associated with significant side effects, including higher rates of lung cancer. To date, structural studies have been confined to individual domains or partially denatured cryo-EM structures. Here we report the cryo-EM structure of the glycosylated full sACE dimer. We resolved four structural states at 2.99 to 3.65 [A] resolution which are primarily differentiated by varying degrees of solvent accessibility to the active sites and reveal the full dimerization interface. We also employed all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and heterogeneity analysis in cryoSPARC, cryoDRGN, and RECOVAR to elucidate the conformational dynamics of sACE and identify key regions mediating conformational change. We identify differences in the mechanisms governing the conformational dynamics of individual domains that have implications for the design of domain-specific sACE modulators.

Dimerization underpins all macromolecular assembly processes both on and off the membrane. While the strength of dimerization, KD, is commonly quantified in solution (3D), many proteins like the soluble BAR domain-containing proteins also reversibly dimerize while bound to a membrane surface (2D). The ratio of dissociation constants, [Formula], defines a lengthscale that is essential for determining whether dimerization is more favorable in solution or on the membrane surface, particularly for these proteins that reversibly transition between 3D and 2D. While purely entropic rigid-body estimates of h apply well to transmembrane adhesion proteins, we show here using Molecular Dynamics simulations that even moderate flexibility in BAR domains dramatically alters the free energy landscape from 3D to 2D, driving enhanced selectivity and stability of the native dimer in 2D. By simulating BAR homodimerization in three distinct environments, 1) solution (3D), 2) bound to a lipid bilayer (2D), and 3) fully solvated but restrained to a pseudo membrane (2D), we show that both 2D environments induce backbone configurations that better match the crystal structure and produce more enthalpically favorable dimer states, violating the rigid-body estimates to drive h<<hRIGID. Remarkably, contact with an explicit lipid bilayer is not necessary to drive these changes, as the solvated pseudo membrane induces this same result. We show this outcome depends on the stability of the protein interaction, as a parameterization that produces exceptionally stable binding in 3D does not induce systematic improvements on the membrane. With h lengthscales calculated here that are well below a physiological volume-to-surface-area lengthscale, assembly will be dramatically enhanced on the membrane, which aligns with BAR domain function as membrane remodelers. Our approach provides simple metrics to move beyond rigid-body estimates of 2D affinities and assess whether conformational flexibility selects for enhanced stability on membranes.

sample_q_texts: Deep-sequencing enables time-resolved gene expression analysis by sequencing many different molecules simultaneously. Recently, DeepTsashi attempts to capture the spatial information from genome-scale gene expression data, improving both resolution and estimation accuracy. This approach only retains highly uniform expression regions and can therefore miss important spatial information, especially in complex biological systems such as multi-cellular organisms. In the current manuscript, we address this limitation by incorporating space-resolving global GeneGO. GeneGO acts as a fusion between the coarse-grained spatial representation from the DeepTsashi scaffold and the fine-resolution gene embedding from the deCODE-Seq database. By averaging over just 5,000 samples, the fused model was able to outperform DeepTsashi by 10-fold, demonstrating improved quantification accuracy, capture of non-uniform expression, and spatial resolution. We validated the model using simulated data and analyzed published genomes to demonstrate its applicability and reliability. Overall, we are hopeful that GeneGO could deliver a powerful tool for spatially resolved and coherent phenome-scale measurement

In cancer biology, single tumor clones are not necessarily representative of the disease progression. The heterogeneity of clones within a tumor complex may originate at several spatial scales. This is in line with the generalization of the Standard Model which has rarely been used at the spatial and clonal levels in cancer research. Here, we present the Cytospectric Model (CSM) - a novel state-of-the-art statistical model that achieves state-of-the-art performance of supervised and unsupervised clustering of single-cell data across a wide range of sizes from 3 to 150 trillion single-cell tissue samples. The CSM integrates information on spatial and clonal structure from tissue spatial measurements to achieve realistic clustering solutions across the heterogeneous tumor complexities that exist in cancer cells. We also demonstrate how the approach promotes in situ tumor segmentation from TCGA datasets. Our results show that the CSM effectively models clonal and tumor complex spatial-hierarchical structure in the technical dimensions of single-cell data, and also reliably merges clusters of highly similar cells together. The CSM is not only superior to other stochastic clustering methods in image classification, but also outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised clustering approaches for massive data from publicly available datasets. Our results show that the CSM is suitable for a variety of cancer studies, particularly, for exploring and understanding the complex spatial structure of tumor genomes. Our findings reveal how a conventional support vector machine can complement deep architectures for biological studies of tissue-size samples, and allows for the characterization of the spatial landscape of whole complexes.

Frame-based descriptors are effective representations of spatio-temporal and geometric patterns of biomedical data. The Discovery Studio (DST) pipeline is an open-source toolbox designed for qualitative exploration and data mining of diverse sets of anatomical, functional, or genomic images. It integrates several scientific software components and uses graph-based algorithms to integrate with a large infrastructure based on Keras and Tensorflow. Thus, the DST pipeline is a flexible framework for exploring biomedicine using graphical decision-making.

Most recently, researchers have begun to utilize DSS1 and its modules for exploring image-based disease prediction, and the Stone et al., 2022, used DST to identify the dynamics of orthore-tric lesions in breast cancer, while the large corpus approach (LC1) combined all imaging protocols of breast CT (two views) to monitor dynamic accumulation of edema and select thresholds which enabled the identification of the time when the lesions first expand and turn malignant.
sample_p_texts: Spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) and spatially resolved proteomics (SRP) data enable the study of gene expression and protein abundances within their precise spatial and cellular contexts in tissues. Certain SRT and SRP tech-nologies also capture corresponding morphology images, adding another layer of valuable information. However, few existing methods developed for SRT data effectively leverage these supplementary images to enhance clustering performance. Here, we introduce stDyer-image, an end-to-end deep learning framework designed for clustering for SRT and SRP datasets with images. Unlike existing methods that utilize images to complement gene expression data, stDyer-image directly links image features to cluster labels. This approach draws inspiration from pathologists, who can visually identify specific cell types or tumor regions from morphological images without relying on gene expression or protein abundances. Benchmarks against state-of-the-art tools demonstrate that stDyer-image achieves superior performance in clustering. Moreover, it is capable of handling large-scale datasets across diverse technologies, making it a versatile and powerful tool for spatial omics analysis.

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has shown remarkable promise in pathology applications, shedding light on the spatial organization of gene expression and its relationship to the tumor microenvironment. However, its clinical adoption remains constrained due to the limited scalability of current sequencing technologies. While recent methods attempt to infer ST from whole slide images (WSIs) using pretrained image encoders, they remain restricted by limited gene coverage, organ-specific training, and the need for dataset-specific fine-tuning. In light of this, we introduce STPath, a generative foundation model pretrained on a large-scale collection of WSIs paired with ST profiles. This extensive pretraining enables STPath to directly predict gene expression across 38,984 genes and 17 organs without requiring downstream fine-tuning. STPath integrates multiple data modalities, including histological images, gene expressions, organ type, and sequencing technology information, within a novel geometry-aware Transformer architecture. Unlike previous methods that directly map WSIs to gene expression, STPath is trained using a masked gene expression prediction objective guided by tailored noise schedules, effectively balancing between capturing gene-gene dependencies and performing high-quality predictions. We evaluate STPath across 6 tasks spanning 23 datasets and 14 biomarkers, including gene expression prediction, spot imputation, spatial clustering, biomarker prediction, gene mutation prediction, and survival prediction. These results demonstrate STPaths strong ability to infer spatially resolved gene expression and reveal crucial pathological structures within tissue samples, underscoring its promise for scalable ST-based pathology applications.

State-of-the-art spatial proteomic and transcriptomic technologies can deeply pheno-type cells in their native tissue environment, providing a high throughput means to effectively quantify spatial relationships between diverse cell populations. However, the experimental design choice of which regions of a tissue will be imaged can greatly impact the interpretation of spatial quantifications. That is, spatial relationships identified in one region of interest may not be interpreted consistently across other regions. To address this challenge, we introduce Kontextual, a method which considers alternative frames of reference for contextualising spatial relationships. These contexts may represent landmarks, spatial domains, or groups of functionally similar cells which are consistent across regions. By modelling spatial relationships between cells relative to these contexts, Kontextual produces robust spatial quantifications that are not confounded by the region selected. We demonstrate in spatial proteomics and spatial transcriptomics datasets that modelling spatial relationships this way is biologically meaningful. We also demonstrate how this approach can be used in a classification setting to improve prediction of patient prognosis.

Advances in spatial profiling have resulted in the generation of multi-omic atlases that span biological scales. In general, multiple workflows are required for image registration, coordinate registration, and spot deconvolution to integrate modalities. To improve the throughput of registration of multi-omic cohorts, we introduce PIVOT, a user-friendly and open-source interface for streamlined nonlinear registration. We demonstrate PIVOTs strengths through registration of three multi-omic datasets, and show comparison of its performance to existing workflows.

The generation of spatial data in biology has been transformed by multiplex imaging and spatial-omics technologies, such as single cell spatial transcriptomics. These approaches permit a detailed mapping of cell populations and phenotypes within the tissue context, which reveals that tissues are complex ecosystems that include multiple organisational structures over different length scales. Quantitative methods for maximising the information that can be retrieved from these images have not kept pace with technological advances in platforms, and no standard methodology has emerged for spatial data analysis. Proposed pipelines are often tailored to individual studies, leading to a fragmented landscape of available methods, and no clear guidance about which statistical tools are best suited to a particular research question.

In response to these challenges, we present MuSpAn, a Multiscale Spatial Analysis package designed to provide straightforward access to well-established and cutting-edge mathematical tools for analysing spatial data. MuSpAn provides easy to use, flexible, and interactive access to quantitative methods developed from mathematical fields that include spatial statistics, topological data analysis, network theory, geometry, probability and ecology. Users can construct custom pipelines from tools across these fields to address specific biological problems, or conduct unbiased exploration of data for discovery spatial biology. In summary, MuSpAn is an extensive platform which enables multiscale analysis of spatial data, ranging from the subcellular to the tissue-scale.

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have revolutionized tissue architecture studies by capturing gene expression with spatial context. However, high-dimensional ST data often have limited spatial resolution and exhibit considerable noise and sparsity, posing significant challenges in deciphering subtle spatial structures and underlying biological activities. Here, we introduce SpaHDmap, an interpretable dimension reduction framework that enhances spatial resolution by integrating ST gene expression with high-resolution histology images. SpaHDmap incorporates non-negative matrix factorization into a multimodal fusion encoder-decoder architecture, enabling the identification of interpretable, high-resolution embeddings. Furthermore, SpaHDmap can simultaneously analyze multiple samples and is compatible with various types of histology images. Extensive evaluations on synthetic and real ST datasets from various technologies and tissue types demonstrate that SpaHDmap can effectively produce highly interpretable, high-resolution embeddings, and detects refined spatial structures. SpaHDmap represents a powerful approach for integrating ST data and histology images, offering deeper insights into complex tissue structures and functions.

Spatially resolved omics (SRO) technologies enable the identification of cell types while preserving their organization within tissues. Application of such technologies offers the opportunity to delineate cell-type spatial relationships, particularly across different length scales, and enhance our understanding of tissue organization and function. To quantify such multi-scale cell-type spatial relationships, we developed CRAWDAD, Cell-type Relationship Analysis Workflow Done Across Distances, as an open-source R package with source code and additional documentation at https://jef.works/CRAWDAD/.

To demonstrate the utility of such multi-scale characterization, recapitulate expected cell-type spatial relationships, and evaluate against other cell-type spatial analyses, we applied CRAWDAD to various simulated and real SRO datasets of diverse tissues assayed by diverse SRO technologies. We further demonstrate how such multi-scale characterization enabled by CRAWDAD can be used to compare cell-type spatial relationships across multiple samples. Finally, we applied CRAWDAD to SRO datasets of the human spleen to identify consistent as well as patient and sample-specific cell-type spatial relationships. In general, we anticipate such multi-scale analysis of SRO data enabled by CRAWDAD will provide useful quantitative metrics to facilitate the identification, characterization, and comparison of cell-type spatial relationships across axes of interest.

We developed an integrated imaging pipeline for spatio-molecular and immunophenotypic tissue analysis, enabling the discovery of molecular markers across spatial scales--from functional tissue units to cell types and neighborhoods. Our approach facilitates single-tissue section analysis, enabling direct cross-modality mining of imaging mass spectrometry and highly multiplexed immunofluorescence microscopy. Demonstrated on human kidney tissue, we identified lipidomic markers of cellular neighborhoods associated with renal cell types and immune cell infiltration.

An important task in the analysis of spatially resolved transcriptomics data is to identify spatially variable genes (SVGs), or genes that vary in a 2D space. Current approaches rank SVGs based on either p-values or an effect size, such as the proportion of spatial variance. However, previous work in the analysis of RNA-sequencing identified a technical bias, referred to as the "mean-variance relationship", where highly expressed genes are more likely to have a higher variance. Here, we demonstrate the mean-variance relationship in spatial transcriptomics data. Furthermore, we propose spoon, a statistical framework using Empirical Bayes techniques to remove this bias, leading to more accurate prioritization of SVGs. We demonstrate the performance of spoon in both simulated and real spatial transcriptomics data. A software implementation of our method is available at https://bioconductor.org/packages/spoon.

Spatial transcriptomics is advancing molecular biology by providing high-resolution insights into gene expression within the spatial context of tissues. This context is essential for identifying spatial domains, enabling the understanding of micro-environment organizations and their implications for tissue function and disease progression. To improve current model limitations on multiple slides, we have designed Novae (https://github.com/MICS-Lab/novae), a graph-based foundation model that extracts representations of cells within their spatial contexts. Our model was trained on a large dataset of nearly 30 million cells across 18 tissues, allowing Novae to perform zero-shot domain inference across multiple gene panels, tissues, and technologies. Unlike other models, it also natively corrects batch effects and constructs a nested hierarchy of spatial domains. Furthermore, Novae supports various downstream tasks, including spatially variable gene or pathway analysis and spatial domain trajectory analysis. Overall, Novae provides a robust and versatile tool for advancing spatial transcriptomics and its applications in biomedical research.

Deep generative models for protein structure generation are fundamental to the advancement of drug design and computational biology. Generation of one current protein sequence can yield two phenotypes, often substantially different: an energy optimised, stable secondary structure (e.g., a beta sheet). These two phenotypes describe different aspects of the protein structure, which often need to be addressed independently when learning from random networks. Given this imbalance, it may be desirable to generate high-confidence protein structure (high-ecos) variants from an initial structured context with the training set and query strand, as opposed to the user-specified coordinates (either via the co-variant property of the query or ligand), which is often only ~50% accurate [1]. In this work, we describe a new general architecture for generative protein structure generation, using basis functions for protein architecture to approximate protein contact maps, trained by an iterative variational autoencoder (VAE) of protein A- and B-forms. This facilitates the search for high-confident structures, while simplifying the design of the formative process to obtain a language for prediction models. Moreover, we show that a simple, two-part prototype of this architecture reliably learned to predict the transition maps, improving the scalability of generative protein structure generation and aligning it with existing generative models.

[1] Wei et al. 2023, Nature Communications 14, 6771 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41436-023-00893).

Accurate simulation of structure-based drug design is indispensable for drug discovery. As the gap between experimental and simulation data widens, how to properly extract useful information from experimental data is a challenging issue. While deep learning (DL) can provide useful guidance for automatically inferring the topological structures of target proteins in the protein interaction network, how to capture the interaction data for target prediction and enhance model predictions is still a promising research topic. In this paper, we propose a dual-stream DL framework for protein structure prediction through graph-based deep learning models, where structural graph visualization and statistical modelling help investigate protein-protein interactions and structure prediction. We develop a dual-stream network framework based on deep learning and measure the prediction performance of the proposed network with different pre-processing steps, and compare the performance of the network with the state-of-the-art protein structure prediction model WoLF-3.0. We found that structure visualization and statistical modelling can improve the predictivity of prediction models on network-based prediction and hypothesis-driven construction. However, this framework requires that the predicted structure is in the support of the target structure, which is constrained by the predictive probability distribution of prediction networks. We empirically demonstrate this by comparing the structures of predicted sub-domains for homologous proteins in shared homologies. Our theoretical analysis also suggests that the hardness of structural recognition for protein structure prediction is governed by the relative size of structurally predicted structures and provides robust structural criteria for the detection of proteins in ligand binding sites.

Cryo-EM structure elucidation of GTPB is one of the most challenging tasks, where reliable resolution and contextual depth information are needed to guide further inferences from the high-throughput structural data. One of the key questions addressed in the field is whether structural datasets can be used to guide the entire pipeline to limit the amount of non-relevant structural data (e.g. small structural regions) and improve the structural alignment and context, e.g. to map protein contacts and associations to cellular functions, whereas structural models are used to derive functions to transport to predictions. This work aims to address these important questions by adopting mathematical representations (including long stochastic bond graphs) that guide the parameter estimates in conjunction with chemical predictors, i.e., predictor information leads to a more appropriate use of structural knowledge for computing inferences using machine learning and machine learning models. Based on our ProteinData2 knowledge resource structure, this work provides high-fidelity chemical predictions using a machine learning approach by learning a convolutional neural network architecture trained on large databases of chemically labeled PDB structures. We performed independent validations with various protein structures to assess the robustness of the method, and achieved overall mean accuracy (i.e., a trade-off between domain specificity and accuracy) of over 90% from masked homology models, independent of the experimental errors, and outperform previous methods such as SHINE (Lecial and co-workers 2022) and Hibercomp. Our method can be broadly applicable for structural prediction in genomics, including for other proteins such as transcription factors, helicases, and effectors (Figure).

Extended projection in silico prediction (EPSIP) is a challenging task which leverages the small molecule set of convolutional molecular dynamics simulations (cMDs) to predict the structure-function relationship of small molecules in proteins which contain intrinsic interactions. In this study we propose the integration of machine learning in the EPSIP workflow to improve structure-function relationships between small molecules and proteins. Our approach, InSILP-based Extended Projection in cMDs (InSILP-IMPD), leverage machine learning (ML) classifiers to select candidate molecules from the set of allowed in silico molecules, thus enhancing the overall capacity of the prediction. We have leveraged ML classifiers for directed selection, hypothesis generation, affinity selection, and test of molecular/inhibitor binders. The high-dimensional and complex large scale data sets of structures of two human small molecules and proteins (440 and 140 3D structures, respectively), collected from the Cdmaps database, were used for investigation. A prototype ML classifier ensemble encompassing Bayes, logistic regression, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and linear support vector machine (SVM), alongside a generative model with smooth approximation and Markov Chain Monte Carlo method (MCMC) were developed and assessed. Our tests showed that inSILP-IMPD augmented with ML classifiers improved structure-function relationships in all tested subtasks. This can advance EPSIP for a better representation of small molecules and proteins in large multi-state systems.

Deep learning has emerged as a promising tool for network pharmacology (NP), which integrates molecular and biological data to predict potential drug target interactions and their mechanisms. Predicting protein-protein interactions (PPIs) is essential for advancing both functional and comparative drug discovery. However, current approaches are heavily reliant on species-specific and computationally expensive datasets, limiting their applicability to diverse organisms. In this work, we introduce ADAPTATION (ADAPT), a publicly available assay capable of predicting protein-protein interactions for many proteins across various species. We validate ADAPT by assessing the performance of four independent scoring models from a structural and biologically diverse dataset - one provided with 10, 30, 50, and 100 protein blocks of experimentally validated functional residues. The validated scoring model achieves Pearson correlation coefficient R2 of 0.68 and AUROC of 0.74 for the protein blocks, with a decrease in Pearson correlation coefficient from 0.69 to 0.37 on average between results for 10, 30, 50, and 100 blocks. ADAPT is publicly available at https://adapt.shh.ai.net.

Virtual screening (VS) is a technique enabling predictive computation to discover drug-like binders of proteins and peptide ligands within specific molecular networks. Although VS is still immature and rife with pitfalls, it provides a framework for integrating synthetic allosteric approaches. However, interactions between molecules are not usually amenable to automated molecular-scale analysis, limiting the potential for consistent and realistic protein property predictions. Here we develop a novel virtual protein-protein interaction network analysis method (Predictor), which combines probability and structure search to efficiently predict large-scale protein-protein interactions and lattice side chains. This approach includes protein sequence and structure co-prediction and protein-protein interaction prediction. We present predictions of two large-scale alpha-helical domains and the 1-3 domain in a peptide x-ray crystallographic structure, with further refinements for protein fragment generation. Predictor provides a powerful, flexible, and inexpensive platform for large-scale synthetic biological search and general purpose image-based interactions.

Protein-protein docking is a powerful tool for mapping and analyzing protein-protein interactions, but many protein-protein interactions are poorly understood and most interactions are ambiguous, making docking difficult. Structural similarity between protein folds helps us search for these ambiguous regions and guide docking. To use structural information, a protein's intrinsic fold needs to be mapped to the protein-protein interactions that it is bound to during the docking process. In this work, we propose a novel model to link structural similarity directly to the intrinsic fold and provide structure priors to constrain the thermodynamic evaluation of the intrinsic fold. This paper also proposes a novel way to select structures with the same intrinsic fold as other target structures, ensuring a complete sequence of predictions. This approach should speed up the process of building and obtaining structural model prior knowledge in protein-protein docking.

Utilizing structural similarity directly as prior knowledge in protein docking enables us to estimate the thermodynamic likelihood of the intrinsic fold as strongly as we can using structures with the same intrinsic folds. We evaluate our model on PDB103 and PDB104 with different protein interfaces. We analyze model predictions for protein-protein interaction models of ion channels, antibodies and proteins. We also compare our model with state-of-the-art methods of intrinsic fold learning.

The computational construction of peptides from gene sequences and their ligands is an important and underappreciated part of modern biology, with applications in fields such as drug design, computational biology and artificial intelligence. However, identifying potential peptides from large gene-ligand space is a time-consuming and error-prone process that is laborious and frequently manually handled. Here, we show how the design of an open source ML pipeline streamlines the peptide generation process for rapid and efficient screening of peptides for drug discovery. Specifically, we identify 48 peptides from 22 gene/protein pairs and benchmark against several top-performing predictor models to quantify the performance of open source massively parallel deep generative diffusion networks (MDPNs) on this task. While remaining highly accurate, MDPNs perform significantly better on datasets with smaller training sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our MLP framework can significantly enhance the efficacy of MDPNs in accurately generating candidate peptides and identifying the desired pattern of drug binding. We used this framework to generate more than 1,000 non-toxic kinase inhibitors for rapid and high-throughput analysis of target-binding.

For protein-based synthesis of carbon-based drugs with good genome-scale planning and cost-effective and environmentally safe chemical reactions, we propose a state-of-the-art AI-driven in silico program named Crs123s to optimize molecules with potential in nature. Our model generated the first efficient architecture for engineering linear cyclic peptides to deliver highly prescribed heavy metal chelators with excellent steric and bioactivity control. We implement Crs123s into the one-site reader-binding affinity predictions of the ligand fitting interface (LFFI) to estimate the ligand competition efficiency for 13 lysine ligands and optimize them by tuning for >1700 binding sites, both by using and not using CRISPR-cas9 editing of active substrate peptide sequences. Our model can expand beyond lysine-based and add function-specific effects of human enzymes into the binding affinity predictions, which greatly accelerates optimization time. Additionally, Crs123s was also applied to remove unwanted disruptive residues from ligand sequences. A high-coverage error mask with 10k queries predicts all interaction-relevant residues and further fine-tunes the interfering segments according to the current resonance structure. Notably, our AI-driven predictions could significantly improve binding affinity and loading capacity of various ligands, even for mutated and partially mutated katanins. Our AI-driven CS123 predicts a -39% affinity change with four mutations on katanins at all substrate-specific sites, despite having 95% of similarity scores across the entire model. We predict the cost of improving each conformation relative to the base state for each mutation. Although there are many structural factors that determine the binding affinity of a katanin, we predict all-atom inputs for the structures of 99% of variants with only 10 structural features and these predictions strongly improve the binding affinity of the resulting katanins. In summary, our model combines well-optimized templates, structure-based interface and binding affinity predictions from spike-and-probe reaction analysis, with cutting-edge AI to generate efficient and synthetic chains for drug discovery and design.

The electron density map of a heteropolymer (an aggregate of polymers) in a protein or lipid has previously been considered to be key information for disease modeling. However, due to limitations in the precision achievable with experimental techniques, this approach typically excludes important conformational information. In this work, we introduce a deep neural network to perform molecular-scale three-dimensional (3D) conformational simulations, leveraging advanced quantitative structural analysis methods and GPU implementations from deformable neural networks. Inspired by GANs, we implement a GAN in which each component is rescaled and downsampled before forward-feeding into a single-layer forward neural network with a multi-head attention mechanism. Our results show that the GAN neural network substantially enhances the 3D conformational map in which the EM curve is substantially smoother and more continuous. Our pipeline achieves a top-10 performance on the complete 2D/3D extended forster–Hamilton-based map using deep training data over the full standard ensemble-based representational ICRAMD (integrated convolutional random masks from generative adversarial networks) over the standard ensemble-based FID (fast imaging diffusion projection) based SMAD (Self-supervised deep formative aid-to-supervised and latent graph attention) parameters. This shows the significant impact GANs can have on high-quality iterative computations.
sample_p_texts: Allostery, the process by which binding at one site perturbs a distant site, is being rendered as a key focus in the field of drug development with its substantial impact on protein function. The identification of allosteric pockets (sites) is a challenging task and several techniques have been developed, including Machine Learning (ML) to predict allosteric pockets that utilize both static and pocket features. Our work, DeepAllo, is the first study that combines fine-tuned protein language model (pLM) with FPocket features and shows an increase in prediction performance of allosteric sites over previous studies. The pLM model was fine-tuned on Allosteric Dataset (ASD) in Multitask Learning (MTL) setting and was further used as a feature extractor to train XGBoost and AutoML models. The best model predicts allosteric pockets with 89.66% F1 score and 90.5% of allosteric pockets in the top 3 positions, outperforming previous results. A case study has been performed on proteins with known allosteric pockets, which shows the proof of our approach. Moreover, an effort was made to explain the pLM by visualizing its attention mechanism among allosteric and non-allosteric residues.

Although several tools have been developed to predict DNA-binding residues based on protein sequences and structures, their performance remains limited, and proteins with crystal structures still represent only a small fraction of DNA-binding proteins. Additionally, the process of extracting handcrafted features for protein representation is labor-intensive. In this study, we combined the strengths of pre-trained protein language models and attention mechanisms to propose a sequence-based method: an attention-based deep learning approach for accurately predicting DNA-binding residues, incorporating a contrastive learning module. Our method outperformed all other sequence-based models across two prevalent benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we developed a structure-based graph neural network (GNN) model to demonstrate the impact of the contrastive module. A common limitation of existing models is their lack of interpretability, which hinders our ability to understand what these models have learned. To address this, we introduced a novel perspective for interpreting our sequence-based model by analyzing the consistency between attention scores and the edge weights generated by the GNN model. Interestingly, our results show that large-scale pre-trained protein language models, together with attention mechanisms, can effectively capture structural information solely from protein sequence inputs.

Building on established methods for molecular docking, structure-based deep learning has recently yielded important advances in virtual drug screening. We present simpatico, a method that follows an alternate approach, based on the field of Representation Learning, to dramatically speed the process of accurate drug screening. Simpatico employs graph neural networks to produce high-dimensional embeddings for the atoms of proteins and small molecules, and uses these embeddings to rapidly produce accurate predictions of the interaction potential for drug candidates with target protein pockets. Simpatico can search a database containing 600 million drugs for good binding candidates to a single protein pocket in 2.5 hours on a single GPU. Despite being >1000x faster than state of the art docking and diffusion-based methods, simpatico is competitive with the most accurate of those methods. We also observe that simpatico embeddings can be used to explore toxicity risk and to identify proteins with similar binding potential. Simpatico is open source software; all code, weights, and data may be accessed at https://github.com/TravisWheelerLab/Simpatico.

Nucleic acid aptamers targeting proteins are becoming increasingly important in biopharmaceuticals and molecular diagnostics. Traditionally, aptamers are discovered through labor-intensive screening of nucleic acid libraries using the SELEX method. However, de novo design approaches without experimental screening remain a significant challenge. Here, we employed deep reinforcement learning to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) agent capable of de novo aptamer design, termed AiDTA (AI-driven Docking-Then-Assembling). First, nucleic acid fragments were docked to the target protein to identify target-binding fragments. Then, AiDTA automatically assembled these fragments into aptamers using the Monte Carlo tree search algorithm and a policy-value neural network to guide the agent in generating aptamers with secondary structures similar to the original constituent fragments. Experimental validation demonstrated that the AiDTA-designed DNA aptamers targeting disease-related proteins exhibited high binding affinities in the nanomolar range, achieving the de novo design of protein-binding aptamers for the first time. Our study establishes a new approach to obtaining protein-binding aptamers for potential applications in biopharmaceuticals and diagnostics.

Proteins have proven to be useful agents in a variety of fields, from serving as potent therapeutics to enabling complex catalysis for chemical manufacture. However, they remain difficult to design and are instead typically selected for using extensive screens or directed evolution. Recent developments in protein large language models have enabled fast generation of diverse protein sequences in unexplored regions of protein space predicted to fold into varied structures, bind relevant targets, and catalyze novel reactions. Nevertheless, we lack methods to characterize these proteins experimentally at scale and update generative models based on those results. We describe Protein CREATE (Computational Redesign via an Experiment-Augmented Training Engine), an integrated computational and experimental pipeline that incorporates an experimental workflow leveraging next generation sequencing and phage display with single-molecule readouts to collect vast amounts of quantitative binding data for updating protein large language models. We use Protein CREATE to generate and assay thousands of designed binders to IL-7 receptor  and insulin receptor with parallel positive and negative selections to identify on-target binders. We discover not only individual novel binders but also features of ligand-receptor binding, including preservation of the IL7R - ligand hydrophobic interface specifically and existence of multiple approaches to contact the insulin receptor. We also demonstrate the importance of structural features, such as the lack of unpaired cysteine residues, toward design fidelity and find computational pre-screening metrics, such as interchain predicted TM scoring (iPTM), while useful, are imperfect predictors as they neither guarantee experimental binding nor rule it out. We use the data collected from Protein CREATE to score designs from the initial generative models. Globally, Protein CREATE will power future closed-loop design-build-test cycles to enable fine-grained design of protein binders.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health threat, underscoring the urgent need for innovative antibiotic discovery strategies. While recent advances in peptide design have yielded numerous antimicrobial agents, optimizing these molecules experimentally remains challenging due to unpredictable and resource-intensive trial-and-error approaches. Here, we introduce APEX Generative Optimization (APEXGO), a generative artificial intelligence (AI) framework that integrates a transformer-based variational autoencoder with Bayesian optimization to design and optimize antimicrobial peptides. Unlike traditional supervised learning approaches that screen fixed databases of existing molecules, APEXGO generates entirely novel peptide sequences through arbitrary modifications of template peptides, representing a paradigm shift in peptide design and antibiotic discovery. Our framework introduces a new peptide variational autoencoder with design and diversity constraints to maintain similarity to specific templates while enabling sequence innovation. This work represents the first in vitro and in vivo experimental validation of generative Bayesian optimization in any setting. Using ten de-extinct peptides as templates, APEXGO generated optimized derivatives with enhanced antimicrobial properties. We synthesized 100 of these optimized peptides and conducted comprehensive in vitro characterizations, including assessments of antimicrobial activity, mechanism of action, secondary structure, and cytotoxicity. Notably, APEXGO achieved an outstanding 85% ground-truth experimental hit rate and a 72% success rate in enhancing antimicrobial activity against clinically relevant Gram-negative pathogens, outperforming previously reported methods for antibiotic discovery and optimization. In preclinical mouse models of Acinetobacter baumannii infection, several AI-optimized molecules--most notably derivatives of mammuthusin-3 and mylodonin-2--exhibited potent anti-infective activity comparable to or exceeding that of polymyxin B, a widely used last-resort antibiotic. These findings highlight the potential of APEXGO as a novel generative AI approach for peptide design and antibiotic optimization, offering a powerful tool to accelerate antibiotic discovery and address the escalating challenge of AMR.

Cyclic peptides exhibit favourable properties making them promising candidates as therapeutics. While the design and modeling of peptides in general has seen rapid advances since the advent of modern machine learning methods, existing deep learning models cannot effectively predict cyclic peptide structures containing non-canonical amino acids (ncAAs), which are often crucial for peptide therapeutics. To address this limitation, we here extend the recent AF3-style model Boltz to cyclic peptides with ncAAs. In addition to the positional encoding offset, we used a simple yet effective extension of the cyclic offset encoding based on AlphaFold3s tokenization scheme that allows the modeling of cyclic peptides with modified residues. On a test set of peptides with ncAAs, our approach outperforms HighFold2 on 13/17 cases, with an average C RMSD of 1.877[A] and an average all-atom RMSD of 3.361[A]. Our results show that the cyclic offset encoding shown for AlphaFold2 generalizes to AlphaFold3-based models and can be extended to incorporate ncAAs, showing potential in the design of novel cyclic peptides with ncAAs for therapeutic applications.

In this work, we present Biophysical Representation of Interfaces via Delaunay-based Graph Embeddings (BRIDGE), a coarse-grained graph neural network that captures embeddings containing meaningful information about protein-protein interactions. The BRIDGE model takes as input graphs defined by the Delaunay tesselation of the individual chains and is pre-trained to predict the Delaunay adjacency at the protein-protein interface. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance in this task. The biophysical information captured by the BRIDGE embedding layer due to this pre-training task can further be used for downstream tasks, including for therapeutically relevant property prediction. We demonstrate the use of these embeddings by training models to predict antibody-antigen (Ab-Ag) affinity and antibody viscosity. These predictors, which require only the structures of the individual molecules in isolation, are especially well suited to large molecule therapeutic applications where complex structures are rarely determined until the very latest stages of a project.

Protein pKa prediction is a key challenge in computational biology. In this study, we present pKALM, a novel deep learning-based method for high-throughput protein pKa prediction. pKALM uses a protein language model (PLM) to capture the complex sequence-structure relationship of proteins. While traditionally considered a structure-based problem, our results show that a PLM pre-trained on large-scale protein sequence databases can effectively learn this relationship and achieve state-of-the-art performance. pKALM accurately predicts the pKa values of six residues (Asp, Glu, His, Lys, Cys, and Tyr) and two termini with high precision and efficiency. It excels at predicting both exposed and buried residues, which often deviate from standard pKa values measured in solvent. We demonstrate a novel finding that predicted protein isoelectric points (pI) can be used to improve the accuracy of pKa prediction. High-throughput pKa prediction of the human proteome using pKALM achieves a speed of 4,965 pKa predictions per second, which is several orders of magnitude faster than existing state-of-the-art methods. The case studies illustrate the efficacy of pKALM in estimating pKa values and the constraints of the method. pKALM will thus be a valuable tool for researchers in the fields of biochemistry, biophysics, and drug design.

Metal ions, as abundant and vital cofactors in numerous proteins, are crucial for enzymatic activities and protein interactions. Given their pivotal role and catalytic efficiency, accurately and efficiently identifying metal-binding sites is fundamental to elucidating their biological functions and has significant implications for protein engineering and drug discovery. To address this challenge, we present SuperMetal, a generative AI framework that leverages a score-based diffusion model coupled with a confidence model to predict metal-binding sites in proteins with high precision and efficiency. Using zinc ions as an example, SuperMetal outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a precision of 94 % and coverage of 90 %, with zinc ions localization within 0.52 {+/-} 0.55 [A] of experimentally determined positions, thus marking a substantial advance in metal-binding site prediction. Furthermore, SuperMetal demonstrates rapid prediction capabilities (under 10 seconds for proteins with[~] 2000 residues) and remains minimally affected by increases in protein size. Notably, SuperMetal does not require prior knowledge of the number of metal ions--unlike AlphaFold 3, which depends on this information. Additionally, SuperMetal can be readily adapted to other metal ions or repurposed as a probe framework to identify other types of binding sites, such as protein-binding pockets.

Single-cell sequencing is a revolutionary technology that offers a powerful approach for analyzing cellular heterogeneity. Its ability to capture high-dimensional cellular profiles and its potential applications across multiple fields make it a groundbreaking tool for understanding the complexity and dynamics of human and animal tissue.

Here, we investigate how single-cell data in diagnostic and predictive contexts can be integrated using machine learning methods. We discuss the potential applications of this approach, such as improving methods for analyzing changes in gene expression, studying target product profiles, and identifying patient-specific cellular heterogeneity for personalized medicine. We demonstrate that integrating single-cell data with machine learning models can improve diagnostics by flagging changes earlier than current technologies, enabling more accurate disease monitoring. Our integrated data analysis helps establish cell profiles as objective tools for precision medicine. Finally, we propose a framework for applying ML algorithms to single-cell data. Our proposed method allows for effective combination of conventional medical images with single-cell data. We use such approach to study heterogeneity in lymphoid organ tissues and develop a metric for reliably predicting immunoglobulin G Abs using a dataset, along with a method to evaluate an antibody "class" for a patient through a comparison of their single-cell data.

Thus, we envision this approach as a powerful tool for promoting a more equitable and personalized approach to health care, especially for rapidly changing conditions like COVID.

HighlightsWe demonstrate a high-throughput, orthogonal approach for integrating and analyzing single cell data for detection of regulatory and dynamic changes.

We apply logistic regression with graph neural networks and transfer learning to individualized changes in immunoglobulins in lymphoid tissues.

We propose a combined metric, based on adaptive sampling and a comparison network, for predicting the immune status of an individual patient.

Deep learning analysis of single-cell transcriptional profiles can increase their interpretability and enable targeted measurements of cellular states. One approach is to derive single-cell expression profiles from images (Fig. 1a), sometimes known as single-cell clustering. A second approach is to generate per-cell gene expression measurements from cell-clustering profiles (Fig. 1b), called centroid-based clustering (CDC). CDC represents an important classification task for single-cell profiling but has been comparatively poorly studied. While centroid-based clustering is available in Apache Spark, only a small number of APIs are supported, many are not integrated, and small fragment sizes preclude analysis using density stacks. This challenge hindered community efforts to study CDC.

We present Epoch Time Clustering (ECT), an image-based CDC method. Because clustering increases cell census rates, single-cell clustering is also less prone to detect high false positives. After embedding, clustering datasets can be up to an order of magnitude faster. To demonstrate ECT, we use enriched human progenitor cell lines to study long non-disjunction potential loss of heterozygosity (MMH) and microtubule polarization (Fig. 2a, top). We show that adding genes with small specificities, aligned using a robust density profile, improves cluster capacity, accuracy and recall. Because cluster sizes with the same performance can be scaled to larger cluster sizes by clustering fractions, ECT also enables investigations of rare patterns, including multiple cell states; e.g., a single fusion event that influences lineage population dynamics.

We have implemented ECT using Spark (major task workloads), Nest (open-source), ImageMagick and Python. We released genome-scale, full-genome clustering datasets with head-to-head data from 32 parallel runthroughs, clustersize data from hundreds of parallel runs (pre-training to reduce processing time) and GPU-optimized code.

Advice to those studying how CDC samples can probe single-cell modes of action.

BackgroundSingle-cell sequencing has revolutionized our understanding of human biology and paved the way for developing new diagnostic technologies. One of the significant applications is cell-typing, which has provided vast information about biological organization of undifferentiated cells. The availability of higher-throughput assays has brought the possibility of defining clonal cell states. However, the availability of 3D tissue slice for single-cell sequencing remains a bottleneck. Our previous work used 3D biological space as a powerful visualization tool. However, it was difficult to apply the space to generate higher-resolution cell shapes, especially challenging to delineate cell positions within the 3D volume.

MethodsWe propose a new space-filling algorithm to generate high-resolution spatial data for cell typing. Using this new technique, the 3D space is an exact fitting model for single-cell types. This technique is named "2D-Funt for X-Val(3D)", where X represents spatial dimension (e.g., cell number) of the image, V represents voxel size (e.g., 1000 × 1000 pixels), and F represents dimensional value. We used this algorithm to generate multiple experimental data of typical dendritic cells (DCs), multiple non-dendritic cells (NDCs), and macrophages in isolated tissues, as well as to generate cell tracing trajectories.

ResultsThe algorithm is highly compact and efficient, greatly enhancing the efficiency of single-cell sequencing, and successfully allows us to visualize multicellular tissues and understand cell spatial distributions.

ConclusionOur platform provides a coherent framework to generate 3D high-resolution and high-accuracy datasets for single-cell sequencing, facilitating single-cell line tracing in different tissues, from viral infections to cancer.

RScripts (https://github.com/CAS-Protocols/CC_UOMT2024_GanLI) are available with the datasets and computational code.

Published as Cohesion in the Machine Learning Systems Conference (https://cc-technology.ai/blog/cmo-cvab/) and in MICRA journal (https://micra.phys.escience.org/).

OutlookCC_UTOP is an accessible and easy-to-use collection system capable of sequencing the full genome of individual cells, multiplexed single-cell sequencing from induced pluripotent stem cells, generating whole transcriptomes or microarrays. With the approach, we aim to generate annotated single cell population atlas of humans (COCO-CC) with high computational and/or biological robustness.

Single-cell RNAseq analysis is crucial to unravel biological processes but is challenging when only single-cell data is available. We developed an annotation tool (named G-Touch) for single-cell RNAseq and demonstrate its impact on improving the annotation of single-cell datasets from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients.

Specific cellular populations within multi-dimensional tissues like IPF and CKD patients are difficult to map due to their morphological heterogeneity, making it challenging for traditional single-cell expression atlases to confidently separate blood and urine, brain and lungs, etc. With G-Touch, we were able to not only have absolute atlases for those groups, but also aggregate datasets across cohorts for a higher statistical accuracy.

We found no true differences in the gene expression between UKBiobank patients with IPF and CKD, as well as indicating no true differences in those patients' subpopulations. Functional pathways identified in the UKBiobank IPF cohort, which were enriched in T cells and monocyte, were even more pronounced in the UKBiobank CKD cohort, suggesting a diverse patient response to IPF. Comparing the UKBiobank IPF with ground-truth markers also highlights underrepresented features within IPF, such as neutrophils, and potentially age-related changes in chromatin modification within the IPF cells.

Furthermore, our results indicate that the underlying mechanism of IPF, lung toxicity, lies in the interaction of microglia with IL-11: the PD-1 inhibitor (CT-P92) offers a more effective approach than IL-11 inhibition. This suggests that targeting the specific signaling pathways within each patient groups or even tissues may contribute to effective IPF treatment.

More study on multi-omic multi-dimensional genetic data is needed to further validate this novel tool and its applicability in the healthcare field.

Naive molecular classification in cell analysis relies on the assumption that highly relevant molecular features are sufficiently available in a given cell population. However, many cell-specific gene-expression differences are only transient or neutral and have no meaningful statistical significance in the context of neutral genes. Here, we propose that the true state of a cell relies on an estimated spatial distribution of specific molecular markers, coupled with our hypothesis that the knowledge of this state is only partly available via the existing cell-selective genotyping techniques. Using unsupervised learning from large, high-resolution cellular image data, we design an unsupervised statistical framework to obtain high-dimensional distributions in our space of highly relevant molecular markers and select the true spatial distribution by quantifying its importance and in-silico experimentally. We demonstrate the feasibility of our method using an example, revealing it requires in-silico data derived from human DNA methylation, multiple molecular markers of gene-cell identities and a relatively large computational budget. Furthermore, we explain the hidden level of spatial information of all cell state types, which drives molecular markers into a state where they improve cellular information summary.

In contrast to public libraries of immune cell feature signatures, almost all single-cell (sc) data are confidential because they represent the data of cell teams instead of individual cells. Unlike conventional bioinformatics pipelines, detailed transcriptional data are more difficult to derive, and microbial pathogens or poor-performing gene copy numbers are easier to hide.

To circumvent this problem, we implement a modular system of machine learning (ML)-based data extraction techniques (ML-DE) for the data-in-transit (DIT) problem from clinical and microbiome sc data. These data include single cell activation profiles (SAPs) and transcription factors (TF) binding patterns (patterns), which reveal community composition of whole organisms (e.g., phylogenetically characterized bacteria) and an organism's cell populations, respectively. In contrast to other state-of-the-art DIT approaches, ML-DE employs principled techniques to eliminate personally identifiable metadata and gene counts.

With De-Identification, Individual, and Retrospective (DIDER), we demonstrate the quantitative prediction and generalizability of biologically meaningful samples. Given 24-hour snapshots of the transcriptomes from 205,468 individual cells, we can predict with precision 100% of the target samples individually and from networks of samples in the literature. We introduce the DIDER environment to analyze SC_DB's single-cell-data, to facilitate the study of different aspects of the human microbiome, and for experiments using different gene-family and cellular compositions.

Two scRNA-seq studies of the bovine kidney found that about 75% of the molecularly distinct cell types are associated with distinct biological processes (Latsa, 2018 and Vignau, 2023), providing the context for uncovering transcriptional changes and gene function profiles associated with these processes. The tissues represent compartments within the kidney complexed by blood and lymphatic fluid, both of which can convey products of diseased or damaged liver as reflected in blood as a signal of disease burden and progress over time. We developed a model that uses a cellular information matrix [Bellow 1] to calculate the effects of each biomarker on each of the 6x,10x, and 100x genes as a function of the biomarker measured and spatial time. The model can be used to characterize disease-specific tissue-specific molecular impact. We showed that the liver is associated with oxidative stress, and the colon is associated with inflammation and/or fibrosis. We also showed that the cells that are highly significant as a function of the biomarkers must have significant noise as measured using scRNA-seq as the spatial dimension, for example, a change in transcription factor activity by as little as 1%, to have a significant effect on the highest activated cell types. In addition, we characterized the importance of cell type type and the changes in the number of genes expressed by the highly activated cells to obtain a reduction in the variability of the affected cells, thus explaining the cellular signature that resulted in the marker being statistically significant.

Real-time Flow Cytometry (RT-FCM) has proven to provide powerful and sensitive tools for cellular identification, localization, and sorting. However, the challenge of integrating an artificial neural network for analysis remains. To tackle this, we propose a hybrid approach that combines the expert-expert and deep generative mechanistic models to construct a two-layer, deep flow cytometry ensemble classifier. This hybrid model integrates the generative component of the deep generative mechanistic model with transfer learning to encode significant flow cytometry information into the deep flow dynamics, thereby improving classification accuracy and generalization capabilities. To evaluate the effectiveness of our framework, we used it to train a single-layer, the traditional deep flow dynamics model, a total of seven models that differ in architecture, flow cytometry channels and gates, and the log-likelihood loss function. Two flow cytometry ensemble classifiers trained using the expert-expert and deep generative mechanistic models, optimized using gradient boosting, achieved average performance scores in the range of 19.91% (individual model) to 27.73% (combined model) on publicly available NC5210 datasets from the TC1 network. This hybrid approach effectively integrated expert and deep generative models to create an innovative and versatile flow cytometry ensemble classifier, offering a new paradigm for real-time flow cytometry analysis.

Effective and scalable exploration and analysis tools are vital for the extraction of insights from large-scale single-cell data. However, current techniques for modeling single-cell studies performed across experimental conditions (e.g., samples, perturbations, or patients) require restrictive assumptions, lack flexibility, or do not adequately deconvolute condition-to-condition variation from cell-to-cell variation. Here, we report that Reduction and Insight in Single-cell Exploration (RISE), an adaptation of the tensor decomposition method PARAFAC2, enables the dimensionality reduction and analysis of single-cell data across conditions. We demonstrate the benefits of RISE across two distinct examples of single-cell RNA-sequencing experiments of peripheral immune cells: pharmacologic drug perturbations and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patient samples. RISE enables straightforward associations of gene variation patterns with specific patients or perturbations, while connecting each coordinated change to single cells without requiring cell type annotations. The theoretical grounding of RISE suggests a unified framework for many single-cell data modeling tasks. Thus, RISE provides an intuitive universal dimensionality reduction approach for multi-sample single-cell studies across diverse biological contexts.

HighlightsO_LIRISE enables tensor-based analysis of single-cell experiments across conditions.
C_LIO_LIRISE separates condition-specific effects from cell-to-cell variation.
C_LIO_LIRISE provides intuitive isolation of patterns into condition-, cell-, and gene-specific patterns.
